item.title: External Validation of a Machine Learning Model for Delirium Risk
item.dc:creator: Joseph I. Friedman
Prathamesh Parchure
Weijia Fu
Satyanarayana Cheertirala
Prem Timsina
Ganesh Raut
Katherine Reina
Josiane Joseph-Jimerson
item.description:
Authors: Joseph I. Friedman, Prathamesh Parchure, Weijia Fu, Satyanarayana Cheertirala, Prem Timsina, Ganesh Raut, Katherine Reina, Josiane Joseph-Jimerson, et al.
Journal: JAMA Network Open; Volume: 9; Issue: 11; Pages: e2642142
Abstract: Importance Although external validation of machine learning (ML)-based delirium risk models is a key stage in the model development pipeline, few published reports exist. Moreover, ML-based delirium risk models commonly degrade in performance during external validation. Objective To examine the performance of a fusion multimodal with natural language processing (NLP) delirium risk stratification model in live clinical practice with cross-hospital external validation. Design, Setting, and Participants This quality improvement study evaluated live clinical deployment of the model among patients 60 years or older who were admitted to non–intensive care units at Mount Sinai Hospital (MSH), with external validation performed at Mount Sinai Morningside Hospital (MSM), from December 1, 2024, to December 31, 2025. Main Outcomes and Measures Primary outcomes were performance of the risk stratification model, assessed by area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC), and monthly delirium detection rates. A 2 × 2 confusion matrix was created, and the 4 cells were used to calculate model performance metrics and compare associated diagnostic yield between premodel deployment and active model deployment periods. Results The overall sample included 33 095 admissions to non–intensive care units at MSM and MSH (mean [SD] age, 74.86 (9.22) years; 15 601 women [47.1%], 17 271 men [52.2%]). A total of 9020 MSM inpatient admissions were assigned a delirium risk score by the risk stratification model during live clinical operations and were compared to 21 186 MSH inpatient admissions that were assigned a risk score by the same model. Age at admission significantly differed between patients at MSM and MSH (MSM: median [IQR] age, 75.79 [68.25-83.88] years vs MSH: 72.62 [66.64-79.65] years; P &amp;lt; .001). Patients from MSM and MSH also significantly differed by sex, race and ethnicity, surgical vs medical primary diagnosis, length of stay, and dementia prevalence rate. Among 11 909 MSM patients, patients in the pre-ML cohort (median [IQR] age, 78.00 [71.00-85.00] years) were significantly older than those in the post-ML cohort (median [IQR] age, 75.79 [68.25-83.88] years) ( P &amp;lt; .001). The AUROC of the model was 0.91 (95% CI, 0.90-0.92) for MSM and 0.94 (95% CI, 0.93-0.94) for MSH. The positive predictive value of the model was 25.9% for MSM and 19.4% for MSH. For MSM, the mean monthly delirium detection rate significantly increased from 9.23% (95% CI, 8.07%-10.38%) to 19.59% (95% CI, 17.32%-21.85%) after model deployment ( P &amp;lt; .001). Conclusions and Relevance In this quality improvement study, an ML-based delirium risk stratification model maintained acceptable discriminative performance during external deployment without retraining and was similar to its performance at the development site without retraining. Model deployment was also associated with increased diagnostic yield but a high false positive rate. These findings provide further evidence of the potential generalizability of the model.

item.title: Body Mass Index, Genetic Predisposition, and Obesity-Related Second Cancer Risk in Cancer Survivors
item.dc:creator: Brigitte A. Pfluger
Fetsum Tekalegn
Ellen L. Mitchell
Adriana Lori
Emily L. Deubler
Lauren R. Teras
Alpa V. Patel
Lauren E. McCullough
item.description:
Authors: Brigitte A. Pfluger, Fetsum Tekalegn, Ellen L. Mitchell, Adriana Lori, Emily L. Deubler, Lauren R. Teras, Alpa V. Patel, Lauren E. McCullough, et al.
Journal: JAMA Network Open; Volume: 9; Issue: 11; Pages: e2642135
Abstract: Importance Excess body weight is an established risk factor for second primary cancers (SPCs) among cancer survivors. Whether genetic susceptibility to higher body mass index (BMI) is associated with the risk of obesity-related SPCs remains unclear. Objective To examine associations of genetic predisposition to higher BMI with the risk of obesity-related SPCs and its joint association with BMI. Design, Setting, and Participants This prospective cohort study used data from the Cancer Prevention Study II Nutrition Cohort, a large prospective study of adults residing in 21 states in the US who were cancer-free at the time of the 1992 survey and responded to biennial follow-up questionnaires starting in 1997. Response rates to the biennial questionnaires ranged from 78.1% to 92.1%. Participants for this analysis included cancer survivors who received a diagnosis of a first primary, nonmetastatic invasive cancer between 1992 and 2015, provided a biospecimen sample, and were followed up through 2017. Analyses were conducted between September 2025 and August 2026. Exposures A polygenic score for BMI (PGS-BMI) and BMI. Main Outcomes and Measures Cox proportional hazards models were used to evaluate associations between PGS-BMI and obesity-related SPC risk, as well as between BMI and obesity-related SPC risk stratified by PGS-BMI tertiles. Results This analysis included 14 309 cancer survivors. Their median (IQR) age at first cancer diagnosis was 72.9 (68.2-77.4) years. Approximately 58.6% (8378) of survivors were male, and 58.6% (8382) had a BMI in the overweight (25 to &amp;lt;30) or obese (≥30) range. During a median (IQR) follow-up of 9.1 (4.6-14.2) years, there were 722 (5.0%) obesity-related SPCs. Compared with survivors in the lowest PGS-BMI tertile, those in the highest tertile had greater risk of obesity-related SPCs (hazard ratio [HR], 1.26 [95% CI, 1.06-1.51]). Obesity was associated with increased risk across tertiles of the PGS-BMI without evidence of interaction ( P = .89 for interaction). Compared with survivors with low genetic predisposition and BMI lower than 25, those with low genetic predisposition and obesity had higher obesity-related SPC risk (HR, 1.59 [95% CI, 1.21-2.09]) and those with high genetic predisposition and obesity had the highest risk (HR, 1.82 [95% CI, 1.38-2.40]). The 10-year cumulative incidence ranged from 3.4% (95% CI, 2.9%-4.0%) to 5.1% (95% CI, 4.3%-5.9%) across joint exposure groups. Conclusions and Relevance In this cohort study of cancer survivors, genetic susceptibility to higher BMI was associated with a modestly increased risk of obesity-related SPCs, whereas obesity was associated with greater risk regardless of genetic predisposition. These findings underscore the importance of weight management for all cancer survivors and suggest that a meaningful proportion of obesity-related SPCs may be preventable.

item.title: Generative Artificial Intelligence and Maternal Health Outcomes in Pregnant and Postpartum Individuals
item.dc:creator: Elizabeth M. Norell
Xiaohe Yue
Heran Mane
Francia Ximena Marin Gutierrez
Neha Pundlik Srikanth
Daniel Smolyak
Pankaj Dipankar
Carson J. Peters
item.description:
Authors: Elizabeth M. Norell, Xiaohe Yue, Heran Mane, Francia Ximena Marin Gutierrez, Neha Pundlik Srikanth, Daniel Smolyak, Pankaj Dipankar, Carson J. Peters, et al.
Journal: JAMA Network Open; Volume: 9; Issue: 11; Pages: e2641062
Abstract: IMPORTANCE Generative artificial intelligence (AI) chatbots are increasingly used to support maternal health, but randomized evidence is limited. OBJECTIVE To evaluate whether access to a generative AI maternal health chatbot improved 12-month maternal health outcomes. DESIGN, SETTING, AND PARTICIPANTS This 2-group randomized clinical trial enrolled 400 participants from October 2023 to December 2024, with 12-month follow-up completed in December 2025. Participants were recruited online across 49 US states and the District of Columbia. Eligible participants were English-speaking, aged 14 years or older, pregnant or parenting an infant younger than 6 months, and self-identified as members of racial and/or ethnic minoritized groups. INTERVENTIONS Participants were randomized 1:1 to receive access to the chatbot or an active control consisting of monthly children’s books. MAIN OUTCOMES and MEASURES Primary outcomes were anxiety and depression symptoms at 12 months measured using the Generalized Anxiety Disorder-7 and Patient Health Questionnaire-9. Secondary outcomes included emergency department visits, pregnancy-related complications, postpartum care checkups, effective contraception use, and sleep duration. RESULTS Among 400 randomized participants, the mean (SD) age was 32.6 (5.1) years; 200 (50%) were parenting an infant at enrollment; and 10 (2%) identified as American Indian or Alaska Native, 80 (20%) Asian, 188 (47%) Black or African American, 57 (14%) multiracial, and 65 (16%) Hispanic or Latino. The AI chatbot was not associated with differences in anxiety scores (adjusted mean difference, 0.10; 95% CI, −0.77 to 0.96) or depression scores (adjusted mean difference, −0.23; 95% CI, −1.05 to 0.59), nor with emergency department visits, postpartum care, contraception use, or sleep duration. Among participants pregnant at enrollment, the chatbot was associated with more self-reported pregnancy-related complications in the secondary 12-month end point analysis, but not in longitudinal analyses. Higher chatbot engagement was associated with longer sleep duration and higher anxiety scores in exploratory within-group analyses. CONCLUSIONS AND RELEVANCE In this randomized clinical trial of pregnant and postpartum individuals from racial and ethnic minoritized groups, access to a generative artificial intelligence maternal health chatbot did not improve maternal anxiety or depression at 12 months compared with an active control. Secondary and exploratory findings should be interpreted cautiously. TRIAL REGISTRATION ClinicalTrials.gov Identifier: NCT06053515

item.title: Gestational Age– and Altitude-Specific Hemoglobin Thresholds and Candidate Windows for Preterm Birth
item.dc:creator: Guanghong Yan
Xin Ning
Xueying Chen
Li Geng
Ping He
Tingting Xiao
Xiaomei Wang
Xiao Nong
item.description:
Authors: Guanghong Yan, Xin Ning, Xueying Chen, Li Geng, Ping He, Tingting Xiao, Xiaomei Wang, Xiao Nong, et al.
Journal: JAMA Network Open; Volume: 9; Issue: 11; Pages: e2642037
Abstract: Importance Maternal hemoglobin is a clinically accessible biomarker of preterm birth (PTB) risk, but abnormal thresholds are inconsistent and do not account for variation by gestational age or altitude. Objectives To evaluate the association between maternal hemoglobin concentration and PTB across gestational ages and altitudes, including PTB subtype, and to define gestational age–specific, altitude-adapted hemoglobin thresholds and assessment windows. Design, Setting, and Participants This multicenter, retrospective cohort study used a multisource database integrating electronic medical records, preconception examination, and geospatial data from 5 medical centers in Yunnan, China, a region with a marked altitudinal gradient, and consecutively included singleton pregnancies delivered between January 1, 2017, and July 31, 2025. Exposure Prepregnancy and prenatal hemoglobin values were assessed. Prenatal measurements were grouped into 2-week intervals (target gestational week ±7 days), with 36 weeks analyzed separately. Main Outcomes and Measures Preterm birth was operationally defined as live birth from 28 weeks 0 days through 36 weeks 6 days of gestation. Results Of 141 943 singleton live births among women (mean [SD] maternal age, 29.7 [4.6] years), 12 607 (8.88%) were PTBs. Maternal hemoglobin measurement showed a gestational age–dependent U-shaped association with PTB, and thresholds varied across gestation. Compared with the intermediate group, a low hemoglobin concentration measured at 13 weeks (&amp;lt;12.00 g/dL; adjusted odds ratio [AOR], 1.46; 95% CI, 1.17-1.80) was associated with PTB, persisting from 27 weeks onward (&amp;lt;11.00 g/dL; AOR, 1.48; 95% CI, 1.25-1.74). A high hemoglobin concentration from 19 weeks onward was associated with PTB (&amp;gt;13.50 g/dL; AOR, 1.28; 95% CI, 1.04-1.55). At high altitude, thresholds were generally higher, and a low hemoglobin concentration from 21 weeks was persistently associated with PTB. Subtype analyses showed earlier low hemoglobin concentration associations for medically indicated PTB and middle- to late-pregnancy high hemoglobin concentration associations for both subtypes. Conclusions and Relevance In this cohort study, hemoglobin thresholds associated with PTB varied across gestation and were generally higher at high altitude; low- and high-hemoglobin assessment windows differed and varied by altitude. These findings may help refine gestational age– and altitude-specific interpretation of routine hemoglobin measurements and PTB risk assessment, pending external validation.

item.title: RELAX Perinatal Digital Intervention to Prevent Increasing Anxiety
item.dc:creator: Colette R. Hirsch
Brittannia Volkmer
Yogini Sawjani
Nathalie Towner
Mary Newburn
Jo Bennett
Laura Bridle
Megan McGovern
item.description:
Authors: Colette R. Hirsch, Brittannia Volkmer, Yogini Sawjani, Nathalie Towner, Mary Newburn, Jo Bennett, Laura Bridle, Megan McGovern, et al.
Journal: JAMA Network Open; Volume: 9; Issue: 11; Pages: e2640518
Abstract: Importance Anxiety disorders affect 1 in 5 pregnant women and birthing people. Cognitive bias modification for interpretation reduces anxiety and repetitive negative thinking (RNT; a risk factor for anxiety) among nonpregnant samples. Objective To evaluate whether adding pregnancy-tailored cognitive bias modification for interpretation to usual maternity care (UC) prevents increased anxiety during pregnancy; reduces anxiety, depression, and RNT before and after birth; and improves functioning before and after birth compared with UC. Design, Setting, and Participants The RELAX (Reducing Levels of Anxiety) 2-arm, parallel-group, multisite, superiority, phase 2b randomized clinical trial recruited participants from June 2023 to July 2024, with final assessment in April 2025. Participants included pregnant individuals in the UK at 16 to 28 weeks’ gestation, with high RNT and up to moderate anxiety, recruited via antenatal clinics or self-referral. Intervention Participants were randomized to the self-led digital intervention (RELAX plus UC), involving twelve 17-minute sessions over 4 weeks, or to UC. Main Outcomes and Measures Assessments took place at baseline before randomization (T0) and 4 weeks (T1), 8 weeks (T2), and 36 weeks (T3; 12-24 weeks after birth) after randomization. The primary outcome was anxiety, as assessed by the 7-item Generalized Anxiety Disorder scale (GAD-7) at T2 and as a secondary outcome at T3. Secondary outcomes included RNT (assessed by the 10-item trait version of the Repetitive Thinking Questionnaire [RTQ-10]), depression (general and perinatal, assessed by the Patient Health Questionnaire–9 [PHQ-9] and Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale [EPDS]), perinatal anxiety (assessed by the Perinatal Anxiety Screening Scale [PASS]), worry (assessed by the Penn State Worry Questionnaire [PSWQ]), and functioning (assessed by the Work and Social Adjustment Scale [WSAS]). Interpretation bias at T1 was the hypothesized mechanism. Analysis was performed using a modified intention-to-treat approach. Results A total of 268 participants were randomized (mean [SD] age 33.7 [3.9] years; 174 [64.9%] married). Anxiety was significantly lower for RELAX participants vs UC (mean GAD-7 difference, –1.5; 95% CI, −2.4 to −0.6; P = .001). Depression (mean PHQ-9 difference, –0.8; 95% CI –1.5 to –0.1; and mean EPDS difference, –1.1; 95% CI, –2.0 to –0.2), RNT (mean RTQ-10 difference, –2.7; 95% CI, –4.5 to –0.9), worry (mean PSWQ difference, –3.6; 95% CI, –5.9 to –1.3), and perinatal anxiety (mean PASS difference, –5.5; 95% CI, –8.2 to –2.8) were significantly lower at T2. Effects on general anxiety (mean GAD-7 difference, –1.0; 95% CI, –1.9 to –0.1), postnatal depression (mean EPDS difference, –1.3; 95% CI, –2.4 to –0.2), and RNT (mean RTQ-10 difference, –2.4; 95% CI, –4.6 to –0.2) were sustained at T3. RELAX promoted more positive interpretations vs UC (mean difference, 2.1; 95% CI, 1.8-2.3) that did not mediate effects at T2 (indirect effect on GAD-7, –0.2; percentile bootstrap 95% CI, –0.4 to 0.1). Functioning did not differ at T2 (mean WSAS difference, –1.0; 95% CI, –2.5 to 0.5) or T3 (mean WSAS difference, –0.8; 95% CI, –2.7 to 1.2), nor did perinatal anxiety (mean PASS difference, –2.1; 95% CI, –5.5 to 1.4), general depression (mean PHQ-9 difference, –0.2; 95% CI, –1.2 to 0.9), or worry (mean PSWQ difference, –1.4; 95% CI, –4.1 to 1.3) at T3. Conclusions and Relevance In this randomized clinical trial, anxiety was lower during pregnancy and postnatally for RELAX plus UC participants compared with those receiving UC. Integrating RELAX into maternity care for those at risk of increased anxiety has potential to improve maternal mental health. Trial Registration https://www.isrctn.com/ISRCTN12754931

item.title: Overall Survival in Adults With Acute Myeloid Leukemia Initiating Quizartinib vs Midostaurin With Chemotherapy
item.dc:creator: Michelle Hyunju Lee
Angela C. Tramontano
Chenyu Lin
Ellen Madarang
Joanna M. Cwykiel
Wyatt McCall
Stephanie Begley
Nayan Hemant Mainkar
item.description:
Authors: Michelle Hyunju Lee, Angela C. Tramontano, Chenyu Lin, Ellen Madarang, Joanna M. Cwykiel, Wyatt McCall, Stephanie Begley, Nayan Hemant Mainkar, et al.
Journal: JAMA Network Open; Volume: 9; Issue: 11; Pages: e2642122
Abstract: Importance Midostaurin and quizartinib are approved with intensive chemotherapy (IC) in patients with newly diagnosed FLT3 internal tandem duplication (ITD)−positive acute myeloid leukemia (AML), but no randomized clinical trials have directly compared them. Objective To compare 1-year overall survival (OS) among patients with FLT3- ITD variant AML initiating IC with midostaurin or quizartinib. Design, Setting, and Participants This multicenter, retrospective cohort study included patients with newly diagnosed FLT3 -ITD variant AML treated at 12 US referral centers between January 1, 2018, and May 31, 2025. Data analysis was performed from January 2026 to August 2026. Exposures Induction therapy with IC plus midostaurin or quizartinib. Main Outcomes and Measures The primary outcome was 1-year overall survival (OS). Secondary outcomes included 1-year event-free survival (EFS), induction response, and hematopoietic cell transplant (HCT) rates at first remission; FLT3 clearance after induction was exploratory. Safety outcomes included rates of febrile neutropenia, infections, intensive care unit use, total parenteral nutrition and granulocyte colony-stimulating factor use, discharge to a rehabilitation facility after index hospitalization, and early mortality. Cox proportional hazards regression models were adjusted for baseline covariates and HCT as time dependent. Results Among 215 patients (median [IQR] age, 56.0 [45.0-65.0] years; 119 [55.3%] female), 127 (59.1%) received midostaurin and 88 (40.9%) received quizartinib. Median (IQR) follow-up was 667.0 (289.0-1368.0) days for midostaurin and 324.0 (168.0-546.5) days for quizartinib, reflecting the latter’s more recent approval. One-year OS was 78.0% for midostaurin and 93.0% for quizartinib (hazard ratio [HR], 0.22; 95% CI, 0.08-0.58; P = .002). The 1-year EFS was 56.0% for midostaurin and 77.0% for quizartinib (HR, 0.43; 95% CI, 0.25-0.74; P = .003). Patients receiving quizartinib had higher rates of composite complete remission (75 [85.2%] vs 93 [73.2%]; P = .03), whereas rates of FLT3 clearance after induction (20 [38.5%] for quizartinib vs 27 [40.3%] for midostaurin; P = .84) and HCT in first remission (47 [53.4%] for quizartinib vs 83 [65.4%] for midostaurin; P = .08) were comparable. Midostaurin was associated with higher intensive care unit use (19 [15.0%] vs 4 [4.5%]; P = .02), discharge to a rehabilitation facility (9 [7.1%] vs 1 [1.1%]; P = .04), and treatment interruptions (32 [25.2%] vs 10 [11.4%]; P = .01). A sensitivity analysis limited to patients treated in 2023 or later (more balanced follow-up) showed directionally consistent but nonsignificant OS and EFS differences. Conclusions and Relevance In this cohort study of adults with FLT3- ITD variant AML, IC plus quizartinib was associated with improved 1-year survival, induction response, and safety compared with IC plus midostaurin.

item.title: Full-Service Mobile Food Markets and Dietary Quality in Low-Income Housing Communities
item.dc:creator: Melissa Lynn Horning
Kristen Skovbroten Gorman
Stephanie Wagner
Jayne Allyn Fulkerson
Melissa Nelson Laska
Julian Wolfson
Jiayi Hu
Yijie Wang
item.description:
Authors: Melissa Lynn Horning, Kristen Skovbroten Gorman, Stephanie Wagner, Jayne Allyn Fulkerson, Melissa Nelson Laska, Julian Wolfson, Jiayi Hu, Yijie Wang, et al.
Journal: JAMA Network Open; Volume: 9; Issue: 11; Pages: e2646816
Abstract: Importance Full-service mobile markets, also known as grocery stores on wheels, may improve diet-related outcomes by bringing low-cost, nutritious food to individuals experiencing low incomes and low food access. Objective To determine the impact of the full-service Twin Cities Mobile Market on dietary outcomes in low-income communities. Design, Setting, Participants This cluster randomized clinical trial was conducted over 3 waves (January 2022 to October 2025) across 12 public or private subsidized housing sites in the Minneapolis-St. Paul, Minnesota, area. Participants were screened for interest in the mobile market. Follow-up assessments began after 6 months of market service. Analyses were finalized September 2026. Intervention Sites were randomized to weekly market service or waiting list control groups. Main Outcomes and Measures Primary outcome: diet quality (Healthy Eating Index-2020 via 24-hour recalls). A priori secondary outcomes: dietary intake (fruit and vegetable, energy, sodium, and percentage of calories from added sugar), food security (18-item US Department of Agriculture Food Security Screening Module), and fruit and vegetable servings procured for the home (validated tracking tool). Adjusted intention-to-treat (ITT) generalized estimating equations were used to assess outcome differences between treatment groups. Results Among 262 adults who enrolled in the mobile market study, 242 participants (mean [SD] age, 66.5 [11.5] years; 156 women [64.5%]) across 12 sites completed baseline assessments and were randomized to mobile market service or waiting list control groups. There were 137 individuals (56.6%) who received Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP) benefits. Sites had a mean (SD) of 18.2 (4.4) weekly transactions (mean of 110 of 1071 households [10.3%]). Of 109 intervention site participants, 47 individuals (43.1%) shopped at the mobile market 1 or more times in implementation months 5 to 6, while 90 of 94 individuals who reported ever using the market (95.7%) reported that they would recommend the market service. Participant retention was 218 of 242 participants (90.0%). In ITT models, the primary outcome of diet quality (adjusted mean difference, 1.25 [95% CI, −1.60 to 4.10]) among 215 participants and 6 of 7 secondary outcomes (fruit and vegetable, energy, and added sugar intake; food security and food security improvement; fruit and vegetable procurement) were not significantly different between groups. Intervention site participants consumed an adjusted mean difference of 397 mg (95% CI, −636 to −158 mg) less sodium daily compared with participants in the waiting list control group. Main findings were consistent across 4 sensitivity and supplemental analyses, except the per-protocol sensitivity analysis, which found that participants in the intervention group consumed an adjusted mean difference of 2.35% (95% CI, 0.66%-4.04%) more calories from added sugar compared with the control group. Conclusions and Relevance In this study, satisfaction with the mobile market was high, but the mobile market did not improve diet quality or most outcomes examined. The mobile market was associated with a meaningful sodium reduction that could improve population-level health. Trial Registration ClinicalTrials.gov Identifier: NCT05672186

item.title: Early Metformin Initiation and Glycemic Outcomes in Gestational Diabetes
item.dc:creator: David Alberto Aguilar Macías
Alberto Alvarez-Iglesias
John M. Ferguson
Aoife Maria Egan
Paula M. O’Shea
Declan Devane
Christine Newman
Robert Patrick McEvoy
item.description:
Authors: David Alberto Aguilar Macías, Alberto Alvarez-Iglesias, John M. Ferguson, Aoife Maria Egan, Paula M. O’Shea, Declan Devane, Christine Newman, Robert Patrick McEvoy, et al.
Journal: JAMA Network Open; Volume: 9; Issue: 11; Pages: e2635700
Abstract: Importance Conventional approaches to analyzing composite end points in clinical trials may not fully capture clinically meaningful treatment effects. Objective To estimate treatment effects of early metformin initiation on clinically ordered glycemic outcomes (insulin initiation and fasting hyperglycemia at gestational weeks 32 and 38) using generalized pairwise comparisons (GPCs). Design, Setting, and Participants This secondary analysis of a double-masked, placebo-controlled randomized clinical trial (conducted from June 2017 through September 2022) at 2 centers in Ireland (1 tertiary hospital and 1 regional hospital) included participants with gestational diabetes based on World Health Organization 2013 criteria. Participants were followed up through 12 weeks post partum. The data analysis was performed between October 18, 2025, and February 2, 2026. Intervention Participants were randomized 1:1 to metformin (maximum dose, 2500 mg) or matching placebo, in addition to usual care. Main Outcomes and Measures Generalized pairwise comparisons were performed using (1) a prioritized hierarchy (insulin initiation, fasting hyperglycemia at week 32, and fasting hyperglycemia at week 38) and (2) nonprioritized analyses of each end point, with overall summaries using equal weights and prespecified clinical weights (0.50, 0.25, and 0.25, respectively). Treatment effect sizes were summarized using win ratio (WR), net treatment benefit (NTB), and win odds (WO). Results Of 535 randomized pregnancies, 526 (262 placebo [49.0%] and 264 metformin [51.0%]; mean [SD] age of participants, 34.4 [4.8] years) had primary outcome data. Prioritized GPCs favored metformin over placebo for the composite outcome (WR, 1.46 [95% CI, 1.13-1.89]; NTB, 13.7 percentage points [95% CI, 4.3-22.8 percentage points]; WO, 1.34 [95% CI, 1.10-1.64]) ( P = .004). The largest separation was observed for insulin initiation (WR, 1.68 [95% CI, 1.19-2.38]; NTB, 12.7 percentage points [95% CI, 4.2-21.0 percentage points]) ( P = .003). Nonprioritized overall summaries favored metformin (WR, 1.53 [95% CI, 1.16-2.01]; NTB, 7.5 percentage points [95% CI, 2.7-12.3 percentage points]; WO, 1.32 [95% CI, 1.10-1.57]) ( P = .002), with consistent clinically weighted results (WR, 1.57 [95% CI, 1.19-2.08]; NTB, 8.8 percentage points [95% CI, 3.4-14.2 percentage points]; WO, 1.39 [95% CI, 1.14-1.70]) ( P = .001). Conclusions and Relevance In this secondary analysis of a randomized clinical trial, prioritized and nonprioritized GPCs yielded statistically significant overall estimates favoring early metformin initiation over placebo across insulin initiation and fasting hyperglycemia outcomes. These findings complement the original primary analysis, provide a more clinically interpretable assessment of the composite outcome, and may inform prospective end point design in future trials. item.title: National Trends in Severe Maternal Morbidity by Insurance and Race and Ethnicity
item.dc:creator: Amelia Srajer
Paul Ronksley
Amity Quinn
Erin Brennand
Amy Metcalfe
item.description:
Authors: Amelia Srajer, Paul Ronksley, Amity Quinn, Erin Brennand, Amy Metcalfe
Journal: JAMA Network Open; Volume: 9; Issue: 11; Pages: e2642154
Abstract: Importance Rates of severe maternal morbidity (SMM) and mortality are rising in the US, disproportionally affecting racial and ethnic minority groups and Medicaid beneficiaries. Contemporary analyses investigating the intersectional impact of insurance and race and ethnicity on SMM are lacking. Objective To examine national trends in SMM and maternal mortality across deliveries and evaluate the intersectional association of insurance type and race and ethnicity with these outcomes. Design, Setting, and Participants This serial cross-sectional study used population-based National Inpatient Sample (a 20% stratified sample of hospital discharges) data on delivery hospitalizations from October 1, 2015, to December 31, 2022, in the US, with analyses completed between July 7, 2025, and January 30, 2026. Exposure Assessment of insurance (private vs Medicaid) and race and ethnicity independently and cross-classified into 10 intersectional groups. Main Outcomes and Measures Primary outcomes were composite SMM, nontransfusion-only SMM, and mortality. Multivariable logistic regression was used to estimate adjusted odds ratios (AORs) for outcomes across insurance, race and ethnicity, and intersectional groups. Results Among 27 341 986 weighted deliveries (mean [SD] maternal age, 29.0 [5.8] years; 6.3% of Asian or Pacific Islander, 16.2% of Black, 22.4% of Hispanic, 0.8% of Native American, and 54.3% of White race and ethnicity), 563 250 (2.1%) were complicated by SMM, 2320 of which (0.4%) resulted in death. From 2015 to 2022, composite SMM rates increased 40.5% (from 175.0 to 245.9 per 10 000 deliveries; P &amp;lt; .001), with 16 of 21 individual complications (76.2%) significantly increasing. Medicaid covered 11 658 119 weighted deliveries (45.5%), and included a greater proportion of Black, Hispanic, and Native American individuals than the privately insured population. Adjusted odds of composite SMM were elevated among all intersectional groups compared with White patients with private insurance (all P &amp;lt; .001). Within each racial and ethnic group, SMM odds were significantly higher with Medicaid vs private insurance (Asian or Pacific Islander: AOR, 1.28 [95% CI, 1.20-1.36]; Black: AOR, 1.13 [95% CI, 1.10-1.17]; Hispanic: AOR, 1.29 [95% CI, 1.24-1.34]; Native American: AOR, 1.44 [95% CI, 1.24-1.67]; White: AOR, 1.23 [95% CI, 1.20-1.26]). Significantly increased odds of mortality were primarily observed for Medicaid-insured Asian or Pacific Islander (AOR, 2.63 [95% CI, 1.25-5.52]), Hispanic (AOR, 1.97 [95% CI, 1.16-3.35]), and White (AOR, 2.15 [95% CI, 1.55-2.99]) patients but not for Medicaid-insured Black patients (AOR, 1.55 [95% CI, 0.99-2.41]). Conclusions and Relevance This serial cross-sectional study of births in the US found that racial and ethnic minority status was independently associated with elevated odds of SMM. Medicaid enrollment further compounded this risk and was associated with maternal mortality, suggesting underlying structural inequities that accompany Medicaid coverage rather than a direct effect of insurance type. Addressing these structural barriers through policy reform, including equitable reimbursement and expanded preconception coverage, is critical to mitigate these maternal health inequities.

David Galloway

Clarivet Torres
Valeria Cohran

Astrela Moore
item.description:
Authors: Wenjing Zong, Vahe Badalyan, David Galloway, Nathan Zev Minkoff, Clarivet Torres, Valeria Cohran, Rebecca Same, Astrela Moore, et al.
Journal: JAMA Network Open; Volume: 9; Issue: 11; Pages: e2641939
Abstract: Importance Small intestinal bacterial overgrowth (SIBO) is a common and clinically important complication of short bowel syndrome (SBS) in children, contributing to feeding intolerance, malabsorption, bloodstream infections, and frequent antibiotic exposure. Diagnostic and management practices vary widely across centers, and no rigorously developed, evidence-informed pediatric-specific guidance currently exists. Objective To develop international, pediatric-specific, expert consensus recommendations for the diagnosis and management of SIBO in children with SBS, with emphasis on diagnostic approach, antibiotic therapy, treatment response, and prevention. Evidence Review A modified Delphi process was conducted between April 4, 2024, and February 18, 2025. A 7-member steering committee reviewed pediatric and adult SIBO literature using the terms small-intestinal bacterial overgrowth , short bowel syndrome , intestinal failure , and pediatric . Because pediatric-specific data were limited and study designs were heterogeneous, systematic reviews and meta-analyses were not feasible. Fifty-five international experts from multidisciplinary intestinal rehabilitation programs in North America and Europe were invited to participate in 3 rounds of anonymous online surveys and 2 in-person moderated consensus meetings. Draft statements were iteratively refined. Consensus was defined a priori as agreement of 75% or greater among respondents. Findings Completed surveys were received from 33 participants in round 1, 38 in round 2, and 28 in round 3. Consensus was achieved on 21 statements involving diagnostic approaches, therapeutic strategies, and monitoring practices. Recommendations addressed the use of breath testing and clinical criteria, indications for empiric antibiotic therapy and cycling, antibiotic selection and duration, and dietary considerations. Symptomatic improvement was considered an acceptable indicator of treatment response. Metronidazole was identified as the preferred first-line antibiotic, and long-term antibiotic cycling was supported for selected patients with recurrent, treatment-responsive SIBO. Collectively, the statements provide a practical framework to support consistent clinical decision-making in pediatric SBS-associated SIBO. Conclusions and Relevance This Delphi-based consensus provides the first international pediatric-specific guidance for diagnosing and managing SIBO in children with SBS. Implementation of these recommendations may reduce practice variability, support more judicious antibiotic use, and improve patient outcomes while establishing a foundation for future research in this high-risk population.

item.dc:creator: Dana R. Sax
Dustin G. Mark
Jie Huang
Agnieszka E. Witkowski
Priya Rao
Hemali A. Sudhalkar

item.description:
Authors: Dana R. Sax, Dustin G. Mark, Jie Huang, Agnieszka E. Witkowski, Priya Rao, Hemali A. Sudhalkar, Joeffrey R. Hatton, Tambria M. Turco, et al.
Journal: JAMA Network Open; Volume: 9; Issue: 11; Pages: e2641859
Abstract: Importance Hospitalizations are costly and may lead to adverse events. Some health systems offer treatment in alternative venues of care for select patients. Objective To describe use and short-term outcomes of emergency department (ED) patients transitioned to noninpatient care settings (ambulatory treatment center [ATC], advanced care at home [ACAH], or emergency department observation unit [EDOU]) compared with inpatient care. Design, Setting, and Participants This retrospective cohort study of ED patients aged 19 years or older was conducted from January 1, 2024, to June 30, 2025, at multisite community ED and inpatient medical centers within an integrated delivery system (Kaiser Permanente Northern California). Included patients had active health plan membership; had an ED visit for heart failure, pneumonia, cellulitis, urinary tract infection, COVID-19, or anemia; and had their care transitioned to an ATC, ACAH program (Kaiser Permanente Advanced Care at Home), EDOU, or inpatient bed. Exposure Treatment venue. Main Outcomes and Measures The main outcomes were care escalation (inpatient admission) for patients treated in an ATC, ACAH program, or EDOU, as well as 7-day ED return visits, 30-day hospitalizations, and 30-day mortality following care completion across all venues. Unadjusted outcome rates are reported. Results This study included 26 618 ED encounters (median patient age, 77 years [IQR, 65-85 years]; 52.6% female). Among 22 755 unique patients, 87.4% had 1 encounter, 9.8% had 2 encounters, and 2.8% had more than 2 encounters. There were 728 (2.7%), 880 (3.3%), 5133 (19.3%), and 19 877 (74.7%) encounters in ATC, ACAH, EDOU, and hospital settings, respectively. One-quarter of patients (25.3%) received care in an ATC, ACAH program, or EDOU. Inpatient admission rates were lower for ATC and ACAH encounters than for EDOU encounters (4.3% [95% CI, 2.7%-5.8%], 5.3% [3.8%-6.8%], and 28.0% [26.8%-29.2%], respectively). Rates of 7-day ED visits were similar across venues (ATC: 10.4% [95% CI, 7.8%-12.9%]; ACAH: 5.3% [3.8%-6.8%]; EDOU: 9.2% [8.4%-10.0%]; and hospital: 8.5% [8.1%-8.9%]). In contrast, 30-day mortality and hospitalization rates were lower among ATC, ACAH, and EDOU encounters than in hospital encounters (30-day mortality: 2.1% [95% CI, 1.0%-3.2%], 1.7% [0.8%-2.6%], 2.8% [2.3%-3.2%], and 5.3% [5.0%-5.6%]; and 30-day hospitalization: 11.4% [95% CI, 8.8%-14.1%], 8.3% [6.3%-10.2%], 12.7% [11.7%-13.7%], and 15.3% [14.7%-15.8%], respectively). Conclusions and Relevance In this cohort study of patients treated in alternative venues of care, one-quarter received care in an ATC, ACAH program, or EDOU. These findings suggest that adoption of novel treatment spaces for appropriately selected patients may allow health systems to focus hospital resources on the patients with the most complex needs.

item.title: Accelerated Approvals and Clinical Evidence for Medications for Children
item.dc:creator: Nuzhat Mahbub
Sujata Purja
Chul S. Hyun
Joseph S. Ross
Reshma Ramachandran
Jae Il Shin
Eunyoung Kim
item.description:
Authors: Nuzhat Mahbub, Sujata Purja, Chul S. Hyun, Joseph S. Ross, Reshma Ramachandran, Jae Il Shin, Eunyoung Kim
Journal: JAMA Network Open; Volume: 9; Issue: 11; Pages: e2641933
Abstract: Importance The US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) accelerated approval (AA) pathway allows early access to therapies for serious or life-threatening diseases based on surrogate end points reasonably likely to predict clinical benefit. In pediatrics, where evidence generation is challenging, the use and performance of this pathway remain underexamined. Objective To characterize preapproval and postapproval studies of drugs granted pediatric AAs. Design, Setting, and Participants This cross-sectional study identified preapproval and postapproval studies for pediatric AAs granted between January 1, 2000, and December 31, 2020. Study characteristics and regulatory outcomes were extracted using publicly available sources, including FDA product labels, approval letters, the postmarketing requirements (PMRs) database, ClinicalTrials.gov, and matched peer-reviewed publications as of August 22, 2026. Exposures Granting of pediatric AA. Main Outcomes and Measures Study characteristics and regulatory outcomes, including time from AA to traditional approval. Results From 2000 to 2020, the FDA granted AA to 26 drugs for 35 pediatric indications (7 pediatric-only, 6 pediatric extension, and 22 combined pediatric-adult). Most approvals were supported by extrapolation, including pharmacokinetic bridging. A total of 47 PMRs were issued, primarily for efficacy verification (28 [59.6%]), 26 (55.3%) of which were fulfilled, contributing to traditional approval for 22 indications (62.9%) after a median of 58.1 (IQR, 44.5-80.1) months. Postapproval studies enrolled more patients than preapproval studies (median, 125 [IQR, 58-304] vs 55 [IQR, 27-119]; P = .004) but maintained enrollment of fewer pediatric patients (median, 11 [IQR, 0-61] vs 13 [0-33]; P = .93). Pediatric-only indications had the longest conversion times and lowest PMR fulfillment rates, accounting for 3 of 4 cases with delayed PMR fulfillment. Conclusions and Relevance In this cross-sectional study of pediatric AAs between 2000 and 2020, approval frequently relied on surrogate end points and extrapolation with pharmacokinetic bridging studies, with limited pediatric enrollment. Although confirmatory studies typically verified efficacy within 4 years, pediatric-only indications experienced persistent delays, underscoring ongoing challenges in timely pediatric evidence generation.

item.title: Spousal Traumatic Brain Injury and Risk of Mortality, Dementia, and Cardiovascular Events
item.dc:creator: Bernadette A. D’Alonzo
Connor A. Law
James R. Pike
Eric L. Stulberg
Alexa E. Walter
Ramon Diaz-Arrastia
Rebecca F. Gottesman
Katherine A. Ornstein
item.description:
Authors: Bernadette A. D’Alonzo, Connor A. Law, James R. Pike, Eric L. Stulberg, Alexa E. Walter, Ramon Diaz-Arrastia, Rebecca F. Gottesman, Katherine A. Ornstein, et al.
Journal: JAMA Network Open; Volume: 9; Issue: 11; Pages: e2641851
Abstract: Importance Traumatic brain injury (TBI) is highly prevalent in older adults. While there is strong and growing evidence that TBI is associated with caregiver burden and psychological health, it remains unclear whether a spouse’s TBI is associated with the long-term health of the uninjured partner. Objective To evaluate whether having a spouse who sustains an incident TBI is associated with risk of mortality, dementia, and major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE) and to assess whether associations differ by sex or survival of the injured spouse after TBI. Design, Setting, and Participants This prospective community-based cohort of married couples was performed at 4 US centers in North Carolina, Mississippi, Minnesota, and Maryland as part of the Atherosclerosis Risk in Communities (ARIC) Study. Of 4506 baseline spousal pairs, 3281 were retained for mortality and dementia analyses and 2740 of these for MACE analyses. Participants contributed person-time from baseline (1987-1989) until incident outcome, death, loss to follow-up, divorce or separation, or administrative censoring on December 31, 2022. Analyses were conducted from November 24, 2025, through August 25, 2026. Exposure Incident spousal TBI (ascertained using self-report, hospitalization surveillance, and linked Centers for Medicare &amp;amp; Medicaid Services data), modeled as a 2-category time-varying exposure (spousal TBI vs no spousal TBI) and 4-category exposure incorporating spousal death. Main Outcomes and Measures Incident all-cause mortality, dementia, and MACE. Cox proportional hazards regression shared frailty models were used to estimate associations adjusted for demographic, clinical, and behavioral characteristics. Results Among 3281 married pairs included in mortality and dementia analyses (among whom, 2740 pairs were included in MACE analyses), the mean (SD) age at baseline was 54.5 (5.5) years, with 3281 female and 3281 male spouses (for a total of 6562 participants). The median follow-up was 19.5 (IQR, 10.6-29.0) years. Spousal TBI was associated with increased risk of mortality (hazard ratio [HR], 1.24 [95% CI, 1.07-1.43]; P = .004) but not dementia (HR, 1.17 [95% CI, 0.88-1.56]; P = .28) or MACE (HR, 1.15 [95% CI, 0.84-1.57]; P = .40). In sex-stratified analyses, associations were similar among males and females. In models incorporating spousal death, mortality risk was higher among individuals whose spouse was alive with a TBI (HR, 1.22 [95% CI, 1.05-1.41]; P = .008), higher among those whose spouse was deceased without a TBI (HR, 1.48 [95% CI, 1.36-1.61]; P &amp;lt; .001), and higher among those whose spouse was deceased with a TBI (HR, 1.27 [95% CI, 1.07-1.52]; P = .006) compared with those whose spouse was alive without a TBI. Results were similar, but less precise, for dementia and MACE. Conclusions and Relevance In this cohort study of married pairs of participants in the ARIC Study, having a spouse who sustained a TBI was associated with a modest but significantly higher risk of mortality in the uninjured partner, whereas findings for dementia and major adverse cardiovascular events were less consistent. These findings suggest that the consequences of TBI may extend beyond injured individuals and support family- and care partner–centered approaches to care.

item.title: Cost-Effectiveness of Remote Symptom Monitoring During Adjuvant Endocrine Therapy in Breast Cancer
item.dc:creator: Xin Hu
Freddie Yang
Andrea N. Curry
Gregory A. Vidal
Teresa M. Waters
Chad Robichaux
Lee S. Schwartzberg
Ilana Graetz
item.description:
Authors: Xin Hu, Freddie Yang, Andrea N. Curry, Gregory A. Vidal, Teresa M. Waters, Chad Robichaux, Lee S. Schwartzberg, Ilana Graetz
Journal: JAMA Network Open; Volume: 9; Issue: 11; Pages: e2641402
Abstract: Importance Adjuvant endocrine therapy (AET) reduces recurrence and mortality for women with early-stage hormone receptor–positive breast cancer, yet long-term adherence is suboptimal, largely due to treatment-related symptoms. Remote patient monitoring (RPM) is a potential strategy to improve symptom management, but evidence of its cost-effectiveness is limited. Objective To evaluate the cost-effectiveness of RPM for women prescribed AET for early-stage breast cancer. Design, Setting, and Participants This economic evaluation used data from the THRIVE trial, which randomized adult women initiating AET to an application (app), the app with tailored feedback, or enhanced usual care (EUC) at a large cancer center with 14 clinics from November 15, 2018, to June 11, 2021. The intervention lasted 6 months, and participants were followed up for 12 months (completed September 19, 2022). Each of the 2 interventions was compared with EUC, with uncertainty assessed using probabilistic sensitivity analyses. Data analyses were performed from February 1, 2025, to September 2, 2026. Main Outcomes and Measures Primary outcomes included costs, which were captured during the 12-month study period from a societal perspective, including medical costs, patient time and travel costs, clinician time costs responding to alerts, and app costs; quality-adjusted life years (QALYs), derived from patient-reported 12-item Short Form Health Survey scores; incremental cost-effectiveness ratios; and incremental net monetary benefit. Results Of 304 participants randomized, 214 had complete data. The mean (SD) age was 58.9 (10.8) years. Mean (SD) total costs were highest for the EUC arm ($11 596.10 [$30 231.95]) compared with the app arm ($6682.15 [$12 963.34]; difference, −$4913.95 [95% CI, −$12 864.27 to $3036.37]) and app plus feedback arm ($11 407.85 [$47 068.42]; difference, −$188.25 [95% CI, −$12 830.16 to $12 453.66]). The mean (SD) estimated QALYs were similar across arms (app, 0.79 [012]; app plus feedback, 0.78 [0.13]; EUC, 0.78 [0.12]). This results in an incremental net monetary benefit of $5813.95 (95% uncertainty interval [UI], −$1860.00 to $16 492.58) for app group and $88.25 (95% UI, −$14 781.73 to $13 849.34) for the app plus feedback group at $100 000 per QALY. Probabilistic sensitivity analyses suggest that the app intervention had a 68.2% to 78.1% probability of being cost-effective compared with EUC across a willingness-to-pay threshold of $0 to $200 000 per QALY, while the app plus feedback intervention had a 53.6% to 70.8% probability of being cost-effective. Conclusions and Relevance In this economic evaluation of RPM for women receiving AET, app-only RPM showed lower costs with similar QALY compared with EUC. Its simpler design may also be more readily scalable than the app plus feedback intervention, supporting its potential as a pragmatic, value-based supportive care strategy in oncology.

item.title: Racial and Ethnic Differences in Access to Alzheimer Special Care Units After Hospitalization
item.dc:creator: Huiwen Xu
John R. Bowblis
Shuang Li
Monique R. Pappadis
Yong-Fang Kuo
James S. Goodwin
item.description:
Authors: Huiwen Xu, John R. Bowblis, Shuang Li, Monique R. Pappadis, Yong-Fang Kuo, James S. Goodwin
Journal: JAMA Network Open; Volume: 9; Issue: 11; Pages: e2643623
Abstract: Importance Older adults with dementia often need nursing home care after hospitalization. Objective To examine whether Black and Hispanic patients have different access to Alzheimer disease special care units (ASCUs) after hospital discharge compared with White patients. Design, Setting, and Participants This was a retrospective cohort study of 100% Medicare fee-for-service claims from January 2018 to February 2020. Participants were Medicare beneficiaries with a prior diagnosis of dementia who were hospitalized or admitted to nursing homes from January 2018 to August 2019. Data analyses were performed from January to July 2026. Exposure The race and ethnicity of a patient. Main Outcomes and Measures The primary outcome was long-term care admission to a nursing home with an ASCU. An unadjusted logistic regression, an unadjusted 2-level (patient-hospital) model, and a multivariable 2-level model were conducted to assess racial and ethnic differences in long-term care admission to a facility with an ASCU and whether patient and hospital characteristics could explain the differences. Results Of the 1 428 849 patients, 130 125 (9.11%) were Black, 77 868 (5.45%) were Hispanic, 1 164 829 (81.52%) were non-Hispanic White, 56 027 (3.92%) were of other races (American Indian or Alaska Native, Asian, and Native Hawaiian or Other Pacific Islander), 839 328 (58.74%) were female, and 1 075 171 (75.25%) were aged 75 years or older. A total of 122 654 patients (8.58%) became long-term care residents within 6 months of hospital discharge, and 19 313 patients (1.35%) were admitted to facilities with an ASCU. In the unadjusted logistic model, Black (relative risk [RR], 0.69; 95% CI, 0.65-0.73) and Hispanic (RR, 0.48; 95% CI, 0.44-0.53) patients had lower probabilities of long-term care admission in a facility with ASCU than White patients. After controlling for the clustering of patients in a hospital, the RR substantially increased to 0.94 (95% CI, 0.88-0.99) for Black patients and 0.78 (95% CI, 0.71-0.85) for Hispanic patients. Further controlling for patient and hospital characteristics slightly reduced these RRs. Disparities for Black patients (RR, 0.89; 95% CI, 0.84-0.95), but not Hispanic patients (RR, 0.93; 95% CI, 0.84-1.02), were also observed in the subcohort of Medicare beneficiaries who became long-term care residents. Conclusions and Relevance The findings of this cohort study suggest that disparities in access to specialized dementia care occur mostly because patients from minoritized racial and ethnic groups are treated at hospitals with low rates of discharge to ASCUs. Efforts to improve dementia care access should focus on enhancing hospital discharge planning and addressing the extra barriers faced by female patients.

item.dc:creator: Katherine Anne Comtois
Luciana E. Hebert
Marija Bogic
Anna Evanson
Barbara Wright
Martina Fruhbauerova
Francine Red Willow
Tony Walking
item.description:
Authors: Katherine Anne Comtois, Luciana E. Hebert, Marija Bogic, Anna Evanson, Barbara Wright, Martina Fruhbauerova, Francine Red Willow, Tony Walking, et al.
Journal: JAMA Network Open; Volume: 9; Issue: 11; Pages: e2639023
Abstract: Importance For American Indian and Alaska Native communities, connectedness and belonging are strengths that may reduce suicide risk. Objective To evaluate the effectiveness of culturally-adapted Caring Contacts combined with optimal available resources (intervention) compared with optimal available resources alone (control) in reducing suicidal ideation, suicide attempts, and suicide-related hospitalizations. Design, Setting, and Participants The CARE study was a blinded, 2-group randomized clinical trial conducted between May 2018 and September 2023 among 5 American Indian and Alaska Native communities in Alaska, the Northern Plains, and the Southern Plains, including 4 tribal communities and 1 tribal health organization. Participants were English-speaking adults (age ≥18 years) self-identifying as American Indian or Alaska Native with active suicidality. Analysis was conducted January through April 2024. Intervention Caring Contacts is a low-cost intervention via brief, nondemanding messages exclusively focused on expressing care and interest sent by text message or greeting card on a pre-determined schedule over 12 months. Main Outcomes and Measures Outcomes included suicidal ideation in the past month (measured using the Suicidal Ideation Questionnaire–Junior [SIQ-Jr]), number of suicide attempts, and suicide-related hospitalizations over 12 months. Retention of active suicidality at follow-up was added as an additional outcome. Results Of 1390 individuals prescreened for eligibility, 1202 consented and were screened for eligibility, and 709 (457 [64.5%] female; mean [SD] age, 35.4 [11.5] years) were enrolled and randomized, including 357 participants in the control group and 352 participants in the Caring Contacts intervention. Most participants (549 [77.4%]) self-identified as American Indian or Alaska Native only, and 160 participants (22.6%) as American Indian or Alaska Native plus another racial group. More than half of participants (392 [55.3%]) were never married. The mean (SD) SIQ-Jr score at baseline was 42.0 (13.8), and 604 participants (85.2%) had ever made a suicide attempt. Overall, 454 participants (64.0%) provided 12-month follow-up data. Between baseline and the 12-month follow-up, both groups showed significant reductions in suicidal ideation (mean [SD] score: Caring Contacts, 41.4 [13.7] vs 22.7 [15.3]; enhanced usual care, 42.5 [13.9] vs 23.1 [14.5]) and participants with a past-year suicide attempt (Caring Contacts, 169 of 352 participants [48.0%] vs 34/240 participants [14.2%]; enhanced usual care 155 of 357 participants [43.4%] vs 39 of 238 participants [16.4%]); however, no statistically significant between-group differences were found. Conclusions and Relevance In this randomized clinical trial of culturally adapted Caring Contacts among American Indian or Alaska Native adults with active suicidality, Caring Contacts did not improve suicidal outcomes beyond optimal available resources alone. Similar improvements in both groups may reflect regression to the mean, the therapeutic impact of compassionate baseline engagement with supportive community staff, or the active components of optimal available resources. Further research should explore these dynamics and other culturally grounded interventions. Trial Registration ClinicalTrials.gov Identifier: NCT02825771

item.description:
Authors: Hana Zahed, Connie Bulos-Salim, Karine Alcala, Shaymaa AlWaheidi, Xiaoshuang Feng, Ying Wang, Alpa V. Patel, Loïc Le Marchand, et al.
Journal: JAMA Network Open; Volume: 9; Issue: 11; Pages: e2641494
Abstract: Importance Approximately one-quarter of lung cancers occur in people who never smoked (PWNS). For smoking-associated lung cancer, blood-based protein biomarkers can improve risk assessment. Objective To identify protein biomarkers for lung cancer among PWNS. Design, Setting, and Participants This nested case-control study from 4 cohorts in the Lung Cancer Cohort Consortium (LC3) was conducted for discovery to identify proteins, and a cohort study was conducted using data in the UK Biobank for replication. Participants were from the US, China, and the United Kingdom and donated blood samples between 1996 and 2010. Lung cancer case-control pairs of PWNS from 4 cohorts in the LC3 were matched by cohort, age, sex, and blood collection date. In addition, 49 291 participants in the UK Biobank were included. Data were analyzed from March 2024 to May 2025. Exposure A total of 2821 circulating proteins measured in prediagnostic blood samples collected up to 5 years before lung cancer diagnosis for cases. Main Outcomes and Measures Primary measures were odds ratios (ORs) for discovery and hazard ratios (HRs) for replication. Results Among 180 case-control pairs of PWNS (360 participants) in the 4 LC3 cohorts, 256 participants (71.1%) were female, and the median (IQR) age at enrollment was 66 (55-70) years. In LC3, using a false discovery rate–adjusted P value threshold of .05, 2 proteins were identified as being associated with lung cancer among PWNS: carcinoembryonic antigen–related cell adhesion molecule 5 (CEACAM5) (OR, 1.65 [95% CI, 1.31-2.09]) and CEACAM6 (OR, 1.72 [95% CI, 1.33-2.22]). Associations for both proteins were successfully replicated among participants analyzed regardless of smoking history across 5 years of follow-up in the UK Biobank (CEACAM5: HR, 1.92 [95% CI, 1.66-2.22]; CEACAM6: HR, 1.86 [95% CI,1.59-2.16]). The correlation between CEACAM5 and CEACAM6 was weak (Pearson ρ = 0.25 in the LC3); therefore, both proteins maintained associations with high relative risks after mutual adjustment. For 36 proteins previously identified as robust markers of smoking-related lung cancer, most showed no evidence of an association among PWNS (median OR, 1.47 [IQR, 1.38-1.61] vs 1.01 [IQR, 0.94-1.13] in smoking-related vs nonsmoking lung cancer). Conclusions and Relevance In this nested case-control study, 2 proteins were identified, CEACAM5 and CEACAM6, that were associated with lung cancer in PWNS. Larger studies are needed to evaluate whether there are additional biomarkers associated with lung cancer in PWNS and whether they can identify PWNS with high lung cancer risk.

item.title: Functional Connectivity at Birth and Longitudinal Neurocognitive Development in Very Preterm Infants
item.dc:creator: Junqi Wang
Wei Jia
Hailong Li
Zhixiu Lu
Mekibib Altaye
Kim M. Cecil
Leanne Tamm
Nehal A. Parikh
item.description:
Authors: Junqi Wang, Wei Jia, Hailong Li, Zhixiu Lu, Mekibib Altaye, Kim M. Cecil, Leanne Tamm, Nehal A. Parikh, et al.
Journal: JAMA Network Open; Volume: 9; Issue: 11; Pages: e2641840
Abstract: Importance Understanding how neonatal functional connectivity at birth is associated with later cognitive performance in infants born very preterm (VPT) may help identify early neuroimaging markers of neurodevelopment. Objective To examine the associations between functional connectivity at birth and cognitive performance at age 2 and 3 years in children born VPT. Design, Setting, and Participants This prospective cohort study included infants born VPT (gestational age ≤32 weeks) from 5 level III and IV neonatal intensive care units in the greater Cincinnati, Ohio, area between September 16, 2016, and November 19, 2019. Maternal, pregnancy, delivery, and infant clinical data were collected from birth through discharge from the neonatal intensive care unit. Participants underwent magnetic resonance imaging at full-term–equivalent age at Cincinnati Children’s Hospital using the same scanner. Image preprocessing and statistical analyses for this study were conducted between January 25, 2025, and July 30, 2026. Main Outcomes and Measures Cognitive outcomes were assessed at corrected age 2 and 3 years using the Bayley Scales of Infant and Toddler Development, Third Edition and the Differential Ability Scales, Second Edition, respectively. Functional connectivity was measured within and between the default mode network (DMN), somatomotor network (SMN), dorsal attention network (DAN), frontoparietal control network, visual network (VIS), and cingulo-opercular network (CO). Associations between neonatal functional connectivity and longitudinal cognitive outcomes were examined using a bayesian hierarchical linear mixed-effects model. Results A total of 257 infants born VPT (mean [SD] gestational age, 29.2 [2.5] weeks; 132 male [51.4%]) were included in the final longitudinal analysis. Stronger neonatal connectivity involving the DMN was positively associated with cognitive performance, including intra-DMN (0.23; 95% credible interval [CrI], 0.06-0.39) and DMN connections with the frontoparietal control network (0.24; 95% CrI, 0.07-0.40), SMN (0.20; 95% CrI, 0.02-0.37), VIS (0.32; 95% CrI, 0.13-0.51), and CO (0.39; 95% CrI, 0.21-0.56). Positive associations were also observed for SMN-VIS (0.27; 95% CrI, 0.12-0.43) and SMN-CO (0.26; 95% CrI, 0.09-0.44) connectivity. The SMN-VIS was the only connection showing a difference between assessments, with a less pronounced association at 3 years than at 2 years (interaction, −0.09; 95% CrI, −0.20 to &amp;lt;0.01). Conclusions and Relevance In this cohort study of infants born VPT, neonatal functional network organization was associated with cognitive performance at corrected age 2 and 3 years. The findings highlight the relevance of distributed connectivity involving the DMN and SMN to later cognitive outcomes and support further investigation of neonatal functional connectivity as an early marker of neurodevelopment.

item.title: Moral Distress Among Abortion-Providing Clinicians After the US Supreme Court Dobbs Decision
item.dc:creator: Jocelyn Wascher
Dana Howard
Marta Bornstein
Katherine Rivlin
item.description:
Authors: Jocelyn Wascher, Dana Howard, Marta Bornstein, Katherine Rivlin
Journal: JAMA Network Open; Volume: 9; Issue: 11; Pages: e2641713
Abstract: Importance Moral distress among abortion-providing clinicians could lead to burnout and attrition from the workforce, worsening reproductive care disparities. Objective To describe situations associated with moral distress among abortion-providing clinicians since the US Supreme Court’s Dobbs v Jackson Women’s Health Organization decision across a range of policy environments. Design, Setting, and Participants For this qualitative study, purposive sampling was conducted from May to December 2023 through listservs and snowball sampling across the US. Participants were clinicians providing abortion care in the US in the year following Dobbs. Data were analyzed from March 2024 to April 2025. Main Outcomes and Measures The primary outcome was determining which situations were associated with moral distress in both protective and restrictive abortion policy environments. Deductive and inductive coding approaches were used to analyze open-ended responses. Results Of 310 respondents completing the full survey (271 women [87.7%]; 132 aged 36-45 years [43.6%]), 160 (51.6%) responded to the optional open-ended question. The 160 respondents described situations associated with moral distress in state policy environments that were both protective and restrictive of abortion. Through thematic analysis, 3 main themes of situations associated with moral distress were identified: (1) bans prohibiting conscientious provision of abortion care; (2) forced adjustments to medical practice, including being forced to provide inaccurate information, substandard care, or to limit care due to resource scarcity; and (3) distress related to the broader national environment. Conclusions and Relevance In this qualitative study, clinicians in both abortion-protective and abortion-restrictive environments reported situations associated with moral distress. Solutions for combating moral distress should be targeted to specific situations and sources, including at institutional, state, or national levels.

item.title: National Institutes of Health Funding for Research About Transgender and Nonbinary Youths
item.dc:creator: Ben C. D. Weideman
Benjamin Parchem
Toli Reigada
G. Nic Rider
item.description:
Authors: Ben C. D. Weideman, Benjamin Parchem, Toli Reigada, G. Nic Rider
Journal: JAMA Network Open; Volume: 9; Issue: 10; Pages: e2641377
Abstract: Importance Research is needed to improve health and well-being for transgender and nonbinary (TGNB) youths (&amp;lt;18 years), including access to gender-affirming medical care (GAMC) and associated clinical outcomes. Investment in TGNB youth research at the National Institutes of Health (NIH) has not been well-characterized even though it has been the source of considerable public debate and recent policy changes to restrict funding. Objective To examine patterns of funding for TGNB youth research at NIH, including trends over time, demographic subgroups, GAMC and other health topics, and geographic distribution. Design, Setting, and Participants This cross-sectional study examined NIH funding for research related to TGNB youths from 2012 to 2024, using the NIH Research Portfolio Online Reporting Tools (RePORTER) database. Awards were included if abstracts explicitly focused on TGNB youth health. This study took place at the University of Minnesota and used publicly available data regarding domestic and international grants administered by NIH. It did not include participants. Exposure NIH funding for TGNB youth research. Main Outcomes and Measures The amount of TGNB youth awards, both as a total and a proportion of the NIH portfolio was calculated. Award characteristics (eg, administering institute) were extracted from NIH RePORTER, and costs were inflation-adjusted to 2024 dollar values. Systematic coding of abstracts characterized demographic subgroups and health topics for each award. Results Between 2012 and 2024, 97 awards and 42 supplements totaling $158.3 million were issued for research about TGNB youths, representing 0.06% of the NIH portfolio. Funding increased over the study period and was concentrated among institutions in states with currently protective GAMC policies. To align funding with estimates of the population size of TGNB youths, investment would need to increase by a factor of 3.5 to 9.8. Nonbinary youths and racially and ethnically minoritized TGNB youths were minimally funded. Common research topics included HIV or AIDS ($68.8 million; 43.5%) and mental health ($78.0 million; 49.3%), with the latter associated with increases in total funding from 2021 onward. GAMC funding ($38.3 million; 24.2%) increased moderately over time. Conclusions and Relevance In this cross-sectional study of NIH awards, research about TGNB youths increased from 2012 to 2024, but it was substantially below population-proportional levels, reflecting historical underfunding and structural barriers in research prioritization.

item.title: Symptom Misrepresentation to Obtain Antibiotics
item.dc:creator: Alistair Thorpe
Andrea Gurmankin Levy
Laura D. Scherer

Julia E. Szymczak
Jeffrey T. Kullgren

item.description:
Authors: Alistair Thorpe, Andrea Gurmankin Levy, Laura D. Scherer, Rachael A. Lee, Julia E. Szymczak, Jeffrey T. Kullgren, Valerie M. Vaughn, William B. Petty, et al.
Journal: JAMA Network Open; Volume: 9; Issue: 10; Pages: e2639559
Abstract: Importance Misrepresentation of symptoms, whether through exaggeration, omission, or fabrication, can represent an important barrier to effective patient-clinician communication and shared decision-making, including in the context of antibiotic treatment. Objective To examine the prevalence, reasons for, and characteristics associated with self-reported misrepresentation of symptoms to obtain antibiotics. Design, Setting, and Participants This survey study recruited a national, nonprobability sample of US adults to participate in an online survey from January 8 to February 13, 2026. Data were analyzed from February to March 18, 2026. Main Outcomes and Measures Outcomes of interest were 2 types of symptom misrepresentation (exaggeration and fabrication) to obtain antibiotics and the reasons underlying these behaviors. Additional questions measured antibiotic-related beliefs, experiences, and behaviors and demographics. Results Of 1371 eligible participants, the final sample included 959 individuals (mean [SD] age of 50.7 [17.6] years; 478 [49.8%] female). Overall, 268 respondents (27.9%) reported ever misrepresenting their symptoms to a clinician to get antibiotics. This included 108 respondents (40.3%) who exaggerated existing symptoms (eg, told their clinician they had a cough for 2 weeks when they only had it for 1 week), 19 respondents (7.1%) who fabricated symptoms (eg, told their clinician they had a fever when they did not), and 141 (52.6%) who did both. Cold-like symptoms (eg, cough, sore throat) were the most frequently misrepresented (176 respondents [65.7%]). The most commonly endorsed reasons for misrepresenting symptoms were illness severity, perceived antibiotic efficacy, returning to responsibilities, and desire for autonomy in their treatment decisions. Younger age (age 18-33 vs ≥65 years: odds ratio [OR], 3.20 [95% CI, 1.58-6.63]; age 34-55 vs ≥65 years: OR, 3.05 [95% CI, 1.55-6.17]), often feeling that clinicians do not take their symptoms seriously (OR, 2.19 [95% CI, 1.49-3.22]), believing that antibiotic resistance is a hoax (OR, 1.98 [95% CI, 1.34-2.93]), reporting more comorbidities (OR, 1.16 [95% CI, 1.05-1.28]), having higher lying-acceptability scores (OR, 1.49 [95% CI, 1.23-1.80]), and needing help reading health materials (OR, 2.40 [95% CI, 1.62-3.54]) were associated with higher odds of reporting symptom misrepresentation to obtain antibiotics. In contrast, dislike of taking antibiotics (OR, 0.89 [95% CI, 0.81-0.99]) and higher antibiotic knowledge (OR, 0.73 [95% CI, 0.58-0.91]) were associated with lower odds of misrepresentation. Conclusions and Relevance In this survey study of US adults, nearly 30% of respondents reported misrepresenting symptoms to get antibiotics from a clinician, most commonly cold-like symptoms. Findings highlight the need for strategies to promote antibiotic knowledge and improve patient-clinician communication to address factors contributing to symptom misrepresentation.

item.title: Clinician Communication Behaviors and Perceived Health Care Discrimination Among Black Patients
item.dc:creator: Ebiere D. Okah
Nao Hagiwara
Kelly Robinson
Elijah Johnson
Abbie Begnaud Muckler
item.description:
Authors: Ebiere D. Okah, Nao Hagiwara, Kelly Robinson, Elijah Johnson, Abbie Begnaud Muckler
Journal: JAMA Network Open; Volume: 9; Issue: 10; Pages: e2641656
Abstract: Importance Perceived racial discrimination has been shown to be associated with lower medication adherence and poorer health outcomes among Black patients. Individuals perceive discrimination when they (1) observe negative behaviors and (2) attribute these behaviors to racial bias; effectively reducing racial discrimination, therefore, entails limiting actions that patients most readily attribute to bias. Objective To examine behaviors associated with Black patients’ attribution of negative behaviors by health care workers to racial discrimination. Design, Setting, and Participants This cross-sectional survey study was conducted at 15 health-oriented events in Minneapolis and St Paul, Minnesota, in 2025. A convenience sample of non-Hispanic Black adults older than 40 years was recruited. Participants who experienced negative behaviors by health care workers were included. Exposures Self-reported experiences of 10 negative behaviors and level of trust in the health care system. Main Outcomes and Measures The primary outcome was attribution of negative behaviors to racial discrimination (ARD). Logistic regressions were used to examine associations between experiencing individual behaviors, sum of negative behaviors, and trust in the health care system with ARD. Results A total of 284 adults were recruited, and 152 who experienced negative behaviors were included. Six observations were removed owing to missing data on patients’ attribution for these behaviors, resulting in a final analytic sample of 146 participants (mean [SD] age, 58.7 [10.9] years; 116 female [79.5%]); 109 participants (74.7%) attributed negative behaviors to racial bias. Greater exposure to negative behaviors was associated with higher odds of ARD (odds ratio [OR], 1.42; 95% CI, 1.14-1.76). Having concerns dismissed (OR, 3.49; 95% CI, 1.57-7.79), being spoken to in a cold or impersonal manner (OR, 5.04; 95% CI, 1.82-13.90), and being stereotyped (OR, 4.22; 95% CI, 1.63-10.93) were directly associated with ARD. Trust in the health care system was not significantly associated with ARD (OR, 0.69; 95% CI, 0.46-1.04). In a multivariable analysis, total negative behaviors remained associated with ARD (OR, 1.39; 95% CI, 1.12-1.73), and trust did not. Conclusions and Relevance In this cross-sectional study of communication behaviors attributed to racial discrimination, experiencing dismissiveness, relational coldness, and stereotyping were associated with Black patients’ attribution of negative behaviors to racial bias. Interventions targeting these behaviors may reduce patients’ experience of health care discrimination.

item.title: Small Area Deprivation and Depression or Anxiety in a Nationwide Cohort
item.dc:creator: Emily White Johansson
Anna Ohlis
Mathias Mattsson
Ahmed Nabil Shaaban
Renee M. Gardner
Susanne Wicks
Emilie E. Agardh
item.description:
Authors: Emily White Johansson, Anna Ohlis, Mathias Mattsson, Ahmed Nabil Shaaban, Renee M. Gardner, Susanne Wicks, Emilie E. Agardh
Journal: JAMA Network Open; Volume: 9; Issue: 10; Pages: e2641218
Abstract: Importance Prior studies suggest increased risk of mental health conditions in deprived residential areas, but robust evidence leveraging nationwide health care and prescription registers, including primary care, with socioeconomic databases is lacking. Objective To examine the association between small-area deprivation and depression or anxiety in people aged 10 to 50 years without recent history of these conditions. Design, Setting, and Participants This nationwide register-based cohort study with sibling analysis was conducted in Sweden January 1, 2015, through December 31, 2023, with analysis completed in January to September 2026. Participants were registered in Sweden throughout the study period, including siblings with discordant-exposure status. Exposure Small-area deprivation in 2015 was defined for 5984 areas using an Index for Multiple Deprivation in Sweden categorized into quartiles. Main outcomes and measures Depression or anxiety was defined as the first diagnosis or the first prescription date if no diagnosis was recorded in the study period. Hazard ratios (HRs) for the outcome through December 31, 2023, were computed using Cox regression models adjusted for confounders. Sibling analyses used stratified Cox regression with robust error variance. We separately tested for interactions between small-area deprivation and age, sex, and urbanicity in the association with the outcome. Results A total of 4 065 375 participants (2 169 625 male [53.4%]; median [IQR] age, 30 [20-41] years), including 1 301 647 siblings, were included. Incidence rates per 1000 person-years for depression or anxiety varied across deprivation levels from 22.8 (95% CI, 22.7-22.9; very low) to 25.6 (95% CI, 25.5-25.7; very high). The HR for depression or anxiety associated with living in the most vs least deprived area was 1.18 (95% CI, 1.17-1.19) and 1.15 (95% CI, 1.13-1.17) in the sibling cohort. Urban (HR, 1.18; 95% CI, 1.17-1.19) and periurban (HR, 1.21; 95% CI, 1.18-1.23) residents in most vs least deprived areas had higher depression or anxiety rates than rural counterparts (HR, 1.11; 95% CI, 1.08-1.14). Conclusions and Relevance In this study, people in the most vs least deprived areas had increased depression or anxiety rates, and the association remained in sibling comparisons. There were increased rates of depression or anxiety associated with living in the most vs least deprived areas of urban and periurban settings compared with rural settings, potentially reflecting worse outcomes in deprived urban areas or less contact with mental health services in remote and rural areas.
