item.title: Surgeon- and Practice-Directed Interventions to Reduce Overtreatment of Low-Risk Thyroid Cancer
item.dc:creator: Sarah E. Bradley
Catherine B. Jensen
J. Denard Thomas
Steven Xie
Elizabeth M. Bacon
Michael A. Rubyan
Brian J. Zikmund-Fisher
Sarah T. Hawley
item.description:
Authors: Sarah E. Bradley, Catherine B. Jensen, J. Denard Thomas, Steven Xie, Elizabeth M. Bacon, Michael A. Rubyan, Brian J. Zikmund-Fisher, Sarah T. Hawley, et al.
Journal: JAMA Network Open; Volume: 9; Issue: 10; Pages: e2641374
Abstract: Importance Overtreatment of low-risk thyroid cancer (LRTC) exists worldwide, with many patients unnecessarily undergoing total thyroidectomy. Effective surgeon- and practice-directed interventions to reduce overtreatment are needed. Objective To identify barriers to and facilitators of implementing surgeon- and practice-directed interventions aimed at reducing total thyroidectomy for LRTC. Design, Setting, and Participants This qualitative study, conducted between June 1, 2024, and February 28, 2025, used a focused ethnography that included semistructured interviews of 19 thyroid surgeons and site visits to 7 community and academic practices where thyroidectomy is performed. Main Outcomes and Measures Participants ranked 6 potential interventions for reducing overtreatment of LRTC and identified implementation barriers and facilitators. Verbatim transcripts were analyzed using thematic analysis to identify the most acceptable aspects of the interventions. Ethnographic field notes provided context for interview results. Results The 19 participants were predominantly male (13 [68.4%]), with a mean (SD) age of 46.6 (8.2) years. Participants’ opinions on the usefulness of the proposed interventions differed. However, when asked to explain their intervention rankings, participants’ reasoning for why they preferred particular interventions followed similar patterns. These patterns led to 3 key themes for the development of an effective intervention: (1) thyroid cancer is complex (a one-size-fits-all approach would not allow for nuanced decision-making); (2) although participants recognized the value of an intervention, they believed interventions were not appropriate for their own practice; and (3) surgeon professional identity can impact practice change, resulting in either reluctance toward practice change or motivation to change. Barriers to implementation observed during site visits were associated with differences in the clinic environment (eg, completing clinical demands, physical infrastructure) and across staffing and staff interactions (eg, presence of trainees, patient-surgeon interactions). Conclusions and Relevance In this qualitative study of thyroid surgeons, key factors were identified for the development of an intervention for reducing overtreatment of LRTC. Participants’ assessment of proposed interventions indicated a successful intervention must be seen as useful, surgeons may be motivated through performance feedback, and the intervention must fit well into the existing surgical workflow. Results demonstrated that an acceptable and effective intervention in this setting may take many forms as long as the intervention considered both behavior change and the end user.

item.title: AI-Generated Draft Response Tool, Message Turnaround Time, and After-Hours Replies Among Health Care Professionals
item.dc:creator: Vincent Jeanselme
Catherine Austin
Jungmi Han
Rachel A. Lewis
Gregory W. Hruby
Karthik Natarajan
Shalmali Joshi
item.description:
Authors: Vincent Jeanselme, Catherine Austin, Jungmi Han, Rachel A. Lewis, Gregory W. Hruby, Karthik Natarajan, Shalmali Joshi
Journal: JAMA Network Open; Volume: 9; Issue: 10; Pages: e2641364
Abstract: Importance Patient portal message volumes have increased, creating substantial administrative burden for clinicians and contributing to after-hours electronic health record work. The Epic In Basket Augmented Response Technology tool generates artificial intelligence–drafted replies to patient messages and has been widely deployed to reduce this burden, yet assessment of efficiency remains limited. Objective To examine the associations of response tool adoption, use, and habituation with message turnaround time and after-hours response. Design, Setting, and Participants This retrospective cohort study was conducted using clinician-level panel regression with individual fixed effects. All first responses to patient portal messages sent at Columbia University Irving Medical Center (CUIMC) between March 1, 2023, and May 15, 2025, were analyzed. Exposure Enterprise-level response tool deployment December 2024. Main Outcomes and Measures The primary outcomes were log-transformed message turnaround time, defined as the elapsed time between patient message submission and first response sent by a clinician, and whether the response was sent outside working hours. Results The analysis included 983 154 responses from 1542 clinicians (770 [49.9%] female) and 272 091 patients (mean [SD] age, 48.1 [21.6] years; 121 370 [44.6%] female) at CUIMC. Response tool adoption was associated with an 8.6% (95% CI, 4.6%-12.9%; P &amp;lt; .001) increase in overall message turnaround time. Using the tool was associated with a significant reduction in turnaround time (−29.5% [95% CI, −34.5% to −24.1%]; P &amp;lt; .001). Turnaround time findings were robust across sensitivity analyses. Response tool use was not associated with an overall reduction of after-hours messaging burden (0.61 [95% CI, −1.02 to 2.24] percentage points; P = .46). However, for test results–related queries received during working hours, response tool use was associated with a reduction in after-hours responses (−3.67 [95% CI, −6.94 to −0.39] percentage points; P = .03), and for all messages received after hours, response tool use was associated with an increase in after-hours responses (4.52 [95% CI, 1.54-7.50] percentage points; P = .003). These after-hours findings were sensitive to the definition of working hours in sensitivity analyses. Conclusions and Relevance In this cohort study, response tool adoption was associated with increased turnaround time. Response tool use was associated with reduced turnaround time and with fewer after-hours responses for test results–related queries received during working hours, but more after-hours responses for messages received outside working hours. These findings suggest that the tool may reduce the barrier to responding to certain messages while not uniformly reducing burden.

item.title: Survival After Risk-Reducing Mastectomy in Patients With Pathogenic Variants in BRCA1 and BRCA2
item.dc:creator: Isabel Beshar
David Viveros-Carreño
Nuria Agusti
Karla Barajas
Kate J. Krause
Maria Angeles Lopez-Olivo
Maria D. Iniesta
Banu Arun
item.description:
Authors: Isabel Beshar, David Viveros-Carreño, Nuria Agusti, Karla Barajas, Kate J. Krause, Maria Angeles Lopez-Olivo, Maria D. Iniesta, Banu Arun, et al.
Journal: JAMA Network Open; Volume: 9; Issue: 10; Pages: e2641231
Abstract: Importance The independent survival benefit of risk-reducing mastectomy (RRM), separate from risk-reducing salpingo-oophorectomy (RRSO), remains uncertain among patients with pathogenic variants (PVs) in BRCA1 and BRCA2 genes. Objective To evaluate the association of RRM, magnetic resonance imaging (MRI)-based screening, and mammography alone with all-cause and breast cancer–specific mortality using RRSO-adjusted estimates. Data Sources MEDLINE, Embase, and Web of Science were searched from January 1, 1990, to May 28, 2026. Search structures, subject headings, and keywords were tailored to each database. Study Selection Inclusion criteria were English-language prospective and retrospective observational studies of adult female patients with PV or likely PV in BRCA1 and BRCA2 who underwent RRM or breast cancer screening (MRI-based with or without mammography, or mammography alone), with RRSO excluded by design or adjusted for in multivariable analysis. Studies including females with prior breast or ovarian cancer were excluded. Data Extraction and Synthesis Study reporting followed Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses 2020 network meta-analysis extension. Two authors independently performed study selection, data extraction, and bias assessment using a risk-of-bias assessment tool (ROBINS-I V2) and a grading approach (Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development, and Evaluation [GRADE]). Frequentist random-effects network meta-analysis was performed with surface under the cumulative ranking curve (SUCRA) estimation. Sensitivity analysis was conducted for the BRCA1 cohort. Main Outcomes and Measures Primary outcome was all-cause mortality. Secondary outcome was breast cancer–specific mortality. All outcomes were analyzed and reported as hazard ratios (HRs) with corresponding 95% CIs. Results Five observational studies with 7937 female patients (median [range] age, 35.9 [unreported] years to 43.4 [32.0-55.7] years) met the inclusion criteria. RRM was associated with lower all-cause mortality compared with MRI-based screening (HR, 0.37; 95% CI, 0.22-0.63) and mammography alone (HR, 0.16; 95% CI, 0.08-0.32). RRM was also associated with lower breast cancer–specific mortality compared with mammography alone (HR, 0.07; 95% CI, 0.01-0.44) but did not have significantly lower mortality than MRI-based screening (HR, 0.26; 95% CI, 0.05-1.35). In BRCA1 -only analyses, RRM was associated with lower breast cancer–specific mortality compared with MRI-based screening (HR, 0.13; 95% CI, 0.03-0.66) and mammography alone (HR, 0.03; 95% CI, 0.00-0.15). SUCRA rankings indicated RRM had the highest likelihood of association with the lowest all-cause mortality (SUCRA value, 99.9%). Risk of bias was critical for 4 studies, and certainty of evidence was rated as very low for all 5 studies. Conclusions and Relevance In this systematic review and network meta-analysis of RRSO-adjusted analyses, RRM was associated with lower all-cause mortality compared with breast cancer screening among females with PVs in BRCA1 and BRCA2 , with the greatest magnitude of association for breast cancer–specific mortality observed in BRCA1 PV carriers. These findings provide less confounded survival estimates to support individualized shared decision-making for RRM.

Journal: JAMA Network Open; Volume: 9; Issue: 10; Pages: e2641487
Abstract: Importance Prior studies have shown that patients treated by female physicians experience better outcomes than those treated by male physicians, but evidence has often focused on surgical populations. The association between physician sex and outcomes among hospitalized medical patients across different health care systems remains less well understood. Objective To examine associations between physician sex and care outcomes among hospitalized medical patients admitted with common medical diagnoses in Ontario, Canada. Design, Setting, and Participants This population-based, retrospective cohort study was conducted between January 1, 2008, and December 31, 2022, among inpatients aged 18 years or older admitted with 1 of 7 common acute medical conditions in Ontario, Canada. Data were analyzed from August 16, 2024, to July 13, 2026. Exposure Physician sex, defined in 2 ways: binary sex of the most responsible physician during hospital admission and proportion of in-hospital days managed by a female physician. Main Outcomes and Measures Primary outcomes were 30-day mortality and hospital readmission. Secondary outcomes included 90-day and 1-year mortality and readmission and index hospital length of stay. Multivariable generalized estimating equations were used to calculate adjusted odds ratios (AORs) accounting for patient-, physician-, and hospital-level covariates. Results The cohort included 958 150 patients (54.3% male; median age, 74 years [IQR, 62-83 years]). After adjustment, care by female compared with male physicians was associated with lower 30-day mortality (12.3% [95% CI, 7.2%-21.1%] vs 13.7% [95% CI, 7.9%-23.8%]; AOR, 0.88 [95% CI, 0.85-0.91]) and hospital readmission (18.6% [95% CI, 17.0%-20.2%] vs 18.9% [95% CI, 17.3%-20.5%]; AOR, 0.98 [95% CI, 0.97-1.00]). When physician sex was operationalized as proportion of in-hospital days managed by a female physician (per 10% increment), greater exposure to care by a female physician was associated with lower 30-day mortality (AOR, 0.93; 95% CI, 0.90-0.97) and readmission (AOR, 0.99; 95% CI, 0.98-0.99). Conclusions and Relevance In this cohort study of hospitalized medical patients, those cared for by female physicians experienced lower 30-day mortality compared with those treated by male physicians. These findings warrant further investigation to elucidate underlying mechanisms and potential differences in physician practice patterns.

item.title: Data Extraction Errors and Diagnostic Conclusions of Meta-Analyses
item.dc:creator: Zixing Huang
Yuan Tian
Ping Gong
Tong Zhang
Hehan Tang
item.description:
Authors: Zixing Huang, Yuan Tian, Ping Gong, Tong Zhang, Hehan Tang
Journal: JAMA Network Open; Volume: 9; Issue: 10; Pages: e2640850
Abstract: Importance Systematic reviews (SRs) are often characterized as being inherently reproducible; however, errors arising from the evidence synthesis process can compromise this assumption and lead to reproducibility failure. Objective To investigate the data extraction errors in diagnostic meta-analyses and the extent to which such errors affect the results of meta-analyses. Evidence Review We included SRs with diagnostic meta-analyses from the Cochrane Library filtered by diagnostic up to May 2023. Data used in the original meta-analyses were extracted from the included SRs and independently reproduced from primary studies. Data extraction errors were identified by comparing datasets and classified by potential mechanism. To assess the consequences, we reanalyzed the meta-analyses using error-corrected data with the same effect estimators and methods. The primary outcomes were the proportions of data extraction errors at the trial, meta-analysis, and SR levels. The secondary outcome was the consequences for diagnostic performance measures (eg, sensitivity, specificity, diagnostic odds ratio [DOR], and area under the curve [AUC]). Analysis was conducted between March and June 2026. Findings A total of 46 SRs, 879 diagnostic comparisons, and 6173 primary studies were included. Data extraction could not be reproduced in 338 studies (5.5%) and affected 137 diagnostic meta-analyses (33.1%) and 34 SRs (73.9%). Numerical error (ie, incorrect values) and inferential error (ie, incorrect derivation from statistics) were the most prevalent error types, accounting for 166 of 412 (40.3%) and 140 of 412 (34.0%) errors, respectively. Mismatching error (ie, mismatching data to groups; 69 of 412 errors [16.7%]) and conceptual error (ie, misaligned reference details; 37 of 412 [9.0%]) were also identified. Among 137 reproduced meta-analyses, large changes were observed in 0.7% meta-analyses for sensitivity (absolute differences, &amp;gt;0.20), 3.6% for DOR (fold-changes, &amp;gt;5.0), and 2.9% for AUC (absolute differences, &amp;gt;0.10). Regression analysis of error location showed that combined false-positive and true-negative errors were associated with higher likelihood of moderate or large DOR changes (OR, 1.11; 95% CI, 1.01-1.22). Conclusions and Relevance In this SR of diagnostic meta-analyses in Cochrane reviews, data extraction errors were common and differentially affected performance measures, highlighting the need to implement rigorous data extraction processes and to consider careful selection of performance measures.

item.title: Financial Functioning Before Mental Health Disclosure to a Retail Bank
item.dc:creator: Anna Trendl
Georgina Bremner
Judith Harrison
David J. Llewellyn
David Leake
item.description:
Authors: Anna Trendl, Georgina Bremner, Judith Harrison, David J. Llewellyn, David Leake
Journal: JAMA Network Open; Volume: 9; Issue: 10; Pages: e2641077
Abstract: Importance Financial functioning is an important dimension of mental health, affecting independence and overall functioning. However, there is uncertainty about how financial functioning evolves over time and across mental health conditions, with current evidence largely relying on survey or experimental data. Objective To evaluate whether financial functioning differs in the period preceding mental health disclosure to a bank and whether differences are shared or condition specific. Design, Setting, and Participants In this case-control study, deidentified banking records from a major UK bank were used to compare financial indicators between individuals with a bank-disclosed mental health condition between January 2019 and August 2025 and controls, matched 1:3. Analyses were conducted between July 2025 and March 2026. Exposures Bank-recorded mental health disclosures mapped to diagnostic groupings of mental, behavioral, and neurodevelopmental conditions. Main Outcomes and Measures A total of 331 monthly financial indicators were used to capture financial functioning. A 2-stage bayesian hierarchical model examined how variation in case-control differences was distributed across financial indicators, conditions, and their interaction. Results The case group comprised 18 428 individuals with mental health disclosures (mean [SD] age, 41.5 [13.9] years; 10 357 women [56%]) and the control group included 64 229 individuals (mean [SD] age, 40.9 [14.5] years; 36 052 women [56%]). Differences in financial functioning were evident up to 36 months before disclosure. Compared with controls, posterior mean estimates for cases showed higher welfare-related income (disability benefits: 0.80; 95% credible interval [CrI], 0.78-0.83), greater financial distress (credit scores: −0.52 [95% CrI, −0.55 to −0.49]; overdraft use: 0.49 [95% CrI, 0.47-0.52]), and more frequent bank interaction (eg, telephone banking use: 0.56 [95% CrI, 0.53-0.58]). Additional differences included higher cash use and reduced spending on self-care and recreational activities among cases (standardized differences ≤0.4 SD units). Variance decomposition indicated that most variation was attributable to differences across financial indicators (SD, 0.11; 88% of total variance), with negligible variation explained by condition (SD, 0.01; &amp;lt;1%) and a small contribution from interaction effects (SD, 0.04; 12%), indicating broadly consistent patterns across conditions. Conclusions and Relevance In this case-control study of bank customers, those who disclosed a mental health condition differed from controls across a range of financial indicators preceding the disclosure, with similar patterns across conditions. The findings suggest that banking data may provide objective measures of financial functioning to inform support strategies in banking and clinical contexts.

item.title: User Interface Designs to Address Cancer Misinformation
item.dc:creator: Allison J. Lazard
Mirian Avendaño-Galdamez
Tara Licciardello Queen
Shelby Lake
Tushar Varma
David Marshall
Hung-Jui Tan
Jacob N. Stein
item.description:
Authors: Allison J. Lazard, Mirian Avendaño-Galdamez, Tara Licciardello Queen, Shelby Lake, Tushar Varma, David Marshall, Hung-Jui Tan, Jacob N. Stein, et al.
Journal: JAMA Network Open; Volume: 9; Issue: 10; Pages: e2641122
Abstract: Importance Misinformation about false and potentially harmful cancer treatments is common on social media. Strategies are needed to encourage reporting to reduce exposure to inaccurate treatment claims. Objective To evaluate the impact of 2 user interface designs (prompts on posts) on intervening and sharing cancer misinformation on social media. Design, Setting, and Participants This 3-group, parallel-group, randomized clinical trial assessed outcomes at 5 time points from March 31 to May 12, 2025. US adults (ages 18-65 years) who had a cancer diagnosis or identified as a cancer caregiver and used social media were recruited from Prolific. Participants interacted with cancer misinformation posts on a simulated realistic social media platform. Data were analyzed from May 13, 2025, to July 27, 2026. Interventions Participants were randomized to cancer misinformation posts shown with social cue–enhanced prompts that specify others’ actions and a review policy, standard prompts, or no prompts (control). Main Outcomes and Measures The primary outcome was a participant flagging a post to intervene. Primary and secondary outcomes included recorded social media behavior (flagging, disliking, liking) and self-reported willingness to flag, dislike, like, comment, and share about the posts. Intervening outside the study platform was also assessed. A separate generalized estimating equations model was used for each outcome. Results A total of 294 individuals (mean [SD] age, 39.3 [11.7] years; 179 [62%] women) with cancer or who were caregivers for individuals with cancer were randomized, with 88 participants receiving social cue prompts, 92 receiving standard prompts, and 114 receiving no prompts. Posts with inaccurate claims were flagged 2 to 3 times more often with social cue (224 of 592 posts [38%]) and standard (180 of 689 posts [26%]) prompts than those without prompts (84 of 675 posts [12%]) (social cue vs control: rate ratio [RR], 3.12 [95% CI, 1.79-5.42]; standard vs control: RR, 2.15 [95% CI, 1.20-3.88]). Prompts led to less sharing behavior (ie, liking: 20 posts [3%] with social cue prompts; 10 posts [1%] with standard prompts) compared with posts without prompts (65 posts [10%]) (social cue vs control: RR, 0.07 [95% CI, 0.04-0.15]; standard vs control: RR, 0.13 [95% CI, 0.04-0.42]). Prompts also led to greater willingness to flag and dislike (intervening) and less willingness to like and share compared with no prompt. Standard prompts led to more flagging on existing social media (outside the study platform) than no prompts. Conclusions and Relevance In this randomized clinical trial of user interface designs, simple prompts encouraged responsible behavior online. Prompts on posts led to more intervening and less sharing of cancer misinformation. Trial Registration ClinicalTrials.gov Identifier: NCT07588607

item.title: Preterm Birth and Birth Weight and Cognitive Performance Among Males Eligible for Military Service
item.dc:creator: Jesper Perälä
Julius Möttönen
Daniele De Luca
Ilari Kuitunen
item.description:
Authors: Jesper Perälä, Julius Möttönen, Daniele De Luca, Ilari Kuitunen
Journal: JAMA Network Open; Volume: 9; Issue: 10; Pages: e2640763
Abstract: Importance Preterm birth and low birth weight are associated with adverse neurodevelopmental outcomes in childhood, but their association with cognitive performance in young adulthood remains incompletely characterized at the population level. Objective To determine whether gestational age and birth weight are associated with cognitive performance during compulsory military service in young adult males. Design, Setting, and Participants This nationwide retrospective register-based cohort study included males born in Finland between January 1, 1987, and December 31, 1998 (N = 350 617), identified using linked national health and military registers. The dataset was based on cognitive testing conducted during military service at a mean age of 19 to 20 years. Preconscription deaths and individuals without military cognitive testing data were excluded. Data analysis was performed from June 1 to December 31, 2025. Exposures Gestational age at birth and birth weight. Main Outcomes and Measures Cognitive performance was measured using the Finnish Defense Forces’ cognitive basic test 1, consisting of verbal, numerical, and visuospatial subtests. Scores were standardized on a 9-point scale (mean [SD], 5.00 [1.96]), with the overall score calculated as the mean of the 3 subtests. Results A total of 192 767 participants were included, of whom 10 016 (5.2%) were born preterm. Individuals born extremely preterm scored lower on the overall cognitive test compared with full-term individuals (mean difference, −0.78 [95% CI, −1.07 to −0.49] points). The groups born very preterm and moderately preterm showed progressively smaller deficits, while those born late preterm showed minimal differences compared with their peers born full term. Associations reached a plateau at approximately 36 to 38 gestational weeks. Similar dose-response associations were observed across birth weight categories, with individuals with extremely low birth weight scoring 0.89 (95% CI, −1.23 to −0.55) points lower than those with normal birth weight. Differences were most pronounced in visuospatial and numerical subtests, whereas verbal performance showed little or no association with gestational age or birth weight. Conclusions and Relevance Lower gestational age and birth weight were associated with poorer cognitive performance in young adulthood in a dose-response pattern, with the largest differences observed among individuals born extremely preterm and with very low birth weight. Late preterm birth was associated with minimal cognitive differences. These findings underscore the long-term cognitive impact of preterm birth.

item.title: Ambient Temperature and Heart Failure Hospitalizations in Older Adults in the US
item.dc:creator: Nathaniel Kuhrt
Ashwaghosha Parthasarathi
Daniel I. Bisno
Kevin Josey
Poonam Gandhi
Melanie Rua
David Robinson
Emily Wo
item.description:
Authors: Nathaniel Kuhrt, Ashwaghosha Parthasarathi, Daniel I. Bisno, Kevin Josey, Poonam Gandhi, Melanie Rua, David Robinson, Emily Wo, et al.
Journal: JAMA Network Open; Volume: 9; Issue: 10; Pages: e2641051
Abstract: Importance The U-shaped association between ambient temperature and cardiovascular mortality is well established. However, limited knowledge exists about the association between ambient temperature and heart failure (HF) hospitalizations, particularly among older adults in the US. Understanding this association is essential to informing climate adaptation strategies and health policies. Objective To assess the association between daily ambient temperature exposure and HF hospitalization among Medicare beneficiaries both nationally and by climate region. Design, Setting, and Participants This time-stratified case-crossover study included older adults (aged ≥65 years) hospitalized for HF between January 1, 2007, and December 31, 2022, based on Medicare claims data. Cases were defined as emergency department visits leading to HF hospitalization with up to 4 controls, or nonevent days, matched for the same patient on day of week, month, and year. The data analysis was performed between June 2025 and August 2026. Exposure Daily mean ambient temperature derived from the Parameter-Elevation Relationships on Independent Slopes Model linked through residential zip code. Main Outcomes and Measures The association between mean temperature exposure and HF hospitalization was estimated nationally and by 9 climate regions (Central, East North Central, Northeast, Northwest, South, Southeast, Southwest, West, West North Central) using conditional logit for distributed lag nonlinear models (reference, 75 °F). A 14-day lag was used for mean temperatures less than 75 °F and 0-day lag for mean temperatures greater than 75 °F. Results A total of 1 517 756 HF hospitalizations from 996 312 patients (mean [SD] age, 78.0 [8.2] years, 60.3% female) were identified. Colder ambient temperatures were associated with increased HF hospitalizations nationally. At the regional fifth percentile temperature compared with 75 °F, the largest associations were observed in the West North Central (n = 17 286 [1.1%]; odds ratio [OR], 1.62; 95% CI, 1.25-2.11), West (n = 107 911 [7.1%]; OR, 1.40; 95% CI, 1.28-1.53), Southwest (n = 30 536 [2.0%]; OR, 1.34; 95% CI, 1.11-1.62), and Northwest (n = 33 353 [2.2%]; OR, 1.34; 95% CI, 1.08-1.65) regions. Temperatures greater than 75 °F were not associated with increased HF hospitalization. Conclusions and Relevance This study found that among Medicare beneficiaries, colder ambient temperatures were associated with increased HF hospitalizations, whereas warmer temperatures were not. The U-shaped temperature-cardiovascular risk association described for cardiovascular mortality and other cardiovascular outcomes did not apply for HF hospitalizations among older adults in the US. These findings suggest that ongoing region-specific surveillance of heat- and cold-related HF hospitalization risk will be essential, particularly in areas with limited adaptive capacity.

item.title: Studies of US Department of Health and Human Services Agency Advisory Committees
item.dc:creator: Erfan Taherifard
Sahil R. Mane
Ngoc-Trang Adrienne Nguyen
Joshua D. Wallach
Jason L. Schwartz
Reshma Ramachandran
Joseph S. Ross
item.description:
Authors: Erfan Taherifard, Sahil R. Mane, Ngoc-Trang Adrienne Nguyen, Joshua D. Wallach, Jason L. Schwartz, Reshma Ramachandran, Joseph S. Ross
Journal: JAMA Network Open; Volume: 9; Issue: 10; Pages: e2641134
Abstract: Importance Federal advisory committees provide external expertise and public input to inform regulatory and policy decision-making across agencies within the US Department of Health and Human Services (HHS). Concerns persist about their use, composition, conflicts of interest (COIs), deliberation, transparency, and influence on agency decisions. Objective To identify and characterize original research studies evaluating the implementation and impact of advisory committees convened by HHS agencies since enactment of the Federal Advisory Committee Act. Evidence Review MEDLINE, Embase, Scopus, HeinOnline, EconLit, SSRN, the National Bureau of Economic Research, the HHS Office of Inspector General, the Government Accountability Office, and Google were searched for English-language original studies published from October 6, 1972, through April 10, 2025. Eligible studies characterized the implementation and impact of advisory committees advising agencies within HHS. Studies were categorized by agency and topic domains: meeting use and management, composition, deliberation content and voting, and regulatory impact and performance. Findings within each topic domain were extracted. Findings Among 146 included studies published between 1974 and 2025, 91 (62.3%) were peer-reviewed research articles and 55 (37.7%) were non–peer-reviewed studies. Most studies examined advisory committees convened by the Food and Drug Administration (FDA; 132 studies [90.4%]), with fewer studies focusing on those convened by the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (5 studies [3.4%]), National Institutes of Health (5 studies [3.4%]), and Centers for Medicare &amp;amp; Medicaid Services (2 studies [1.4%]). Meeting use and management was the most commonly examined topic domain (98 studies [67.1%]). Five of the 13 secondary topic domains (38.5%) included only FDA studies, and no secondary topic domain included more than 2 studies (1.4%) on any single non-FDA HHS agency. Key findings included continued use of FDA advisory committees over time despite wide variation across product types and a decline after 2010, a recent increase in FDA advisory committee members’ COIs after a substantial decline following the FDA Amendments Act, and generally high concordance between advisory committee recommendations and agency decisions. Conclusions and Relevance In this systematic review of original research studies, evidence on HHS advisory committees was concentrated largely on those convened by FDA. Variation in advisory committee use and management, ongoing COI concerns, and limited evidence on advisory committees convened by HHS agencies other than FDA suggest opportunities for reform and the need for more studies evaluating advisory committee implementation and impact across HHS.

item.title: Organ Preservation With Watch and Wait in Patients With Rectal Cancer
item.dc:creator: Stephanie S. Keeling
Ramy Behman
Chung-Yuan Hu
John K. Lin
Naveen Manisundaram
Jeongyoon Moon
Brian K. Bednarski

item.description:
Authors: Stephanie S. Keeling, Ramy Behman, Chung-Yuan Hu, John K. Lin, Naveen Manisundaram, Jeongyoon Moon, Brian K. Bednarski, Tsuyoshi Konishi, et al.
Journal: JAMA Network Open; Volume: 9; Issue: 10; Pages: e2640267
Abstract: Importance With growing evidence and evolving guidelines, organ preservation with watch and wait for stage II to III rectal cancer after neoadjuvant therapy is increasingly implemented. However, the true frequency of watch-and-wait use is unknown. Objective To estimate rates of intentional organ preservation with watch and wait by evaluating secular trends across age groups. Design, Setting, and Participants This retrospective cohort study used data from the National Cancer Database (NCDB), with analyses conducted in September 2025. Patients with stage II to III rectal cancer diagnosed between 2006 and 2023 who received neoadjuvant chemoradiation in Commission on Cancer–accredited hospitals participating in the NCDB across the US were included. Exposure Age, year of diagnosis, and treatment strategy (proctectomy vs nonsurgical management). Main Outcomes and Measures The primary outcome consisted of watch-and-wait rates, defined as excess nonsurgical management greater than baseline. To account for nonsurgical management unrelated to the decision for watch and wait, joinpoint regression estimated baseline rates of nonsurgical management and annual percentage changes. A secondary analysis examined associations of age and year with watch-and-wait rates using multivariable logistic regression. Results Among 101 001 patients with rectal cancer (median [IQR] age, 60 [51-69] years; 37 957 female [37.58%]), 84 324 underwent surgery and 16 677 did not. Baseline rates of nonsurgical management remained stable through 2014. Joinpoints occurred in 2014 and 2019, with annual percentage changes of −0.45% (95% CI, −2.26% to 0.78%; P = .42) in 2006 to 2014, 9.83% (95% CI, 4.66% to 13.73%; P = .001) in 2015 to 2018, and 21.71% (95% CI, 17.74% to 29.57%; P &amp;lt; .001) in 2019 to 2023. Baseline nonsurgical management increased with age, from 1331 of 19 785 patients younger than 50 years (6.73%) to 1748 of 6210 patients aged 80 years and older (28.15%). Earlier adoption occurred in older patients; the group aged 80 years and older surpassed 5–percentage point excess watch and wait by 2015 (33.78% annual rate vs 28.15% baseline rate [5.63–percentage point excess]) and 10% by 2017 (39.56% annual rate vs 28.15% baseline rate [11.41–percentage point excess]), compared with 2019 (12.88% annual rate vs 6.73% baseline rate [6.15–percentage point excess]) and 2021 (20.75% annual rate vs 6.73% baseline rate [14.02%] excess) in patients younger than 50 years. Overall, watch and wait increased from 140 of 6101 patients (2.30%) in 2015 to 2068 of 6280 patients (32.94%) in 2023. Increasing year (odds ratio for 2023 vs 2006, 6.23; 95% CI, 5.48 to 7.09) and older age (odds ratio for ages ≥80 vs &amp;lt;50 years, 4.25; 95% CI, 3.98 to 4.54) were independently associated with nonsurgical management (both P &amp;lt; .001). Conclusions and Relevance In this study, watch-and-wait rates increased across all age groups, with a marked acceleration after 2019 suggesting evidence-concordant adoption of the watch-and-wait approach. This underscores the need for careful patient selection, accurate clinical response assessment, and rigorous surveillance monitoring to ensure safe oncologic outcomes.

item.title: Bias-Adjusted Prevalence of Chronic Traumatic Encephalopathy Among Deceased National Football League Players
item.dc:creator: Julia Gallini
Michael L. Alosco
Bobak Abdolmohammadi
Jennifer Weuve
Ann C. McKee
Thor D. Stein
Robert A. Stern
Daniel H. Daneshvar
item.description:
Authors: Julia Gallini, Michael L. Alosco, Bobak Abdolmohammadi, Jennifer Weuve, Ann C. McKee, Thor D. Stein, Robert A. Stern, Daniel H. Daneshvar, et al.
Journal: JAMA Network Open; Volume: 9; Issue: 10; Pages: e2640884
Abstract: Importance The majority of knowledge regarding chronic traumatic encephalopathy (CTE) in National Football League (NFL) players is derived from autopsy-based studies on voluntarily donated brains. Because these cohorts are highly vulnerable to selection bias (specifically registry bias), population-level prevalence of CTE among former NFL players is unknown, limiting understanding of the impact of this disease. Objective To estimate the selection-bias adjusted prevalence of CTE neuropathology in deceased NFL players. Design, Setting, and Participants This population-based cross-sectional study used Understanding Neurologic Injury and Traumatic Encephalopathy (UNITE) brain bank data combined with National Death Index records on former NFL players. Both brain donor and nondonor NFL players who died between January 2008 and December 2023 were included. Data were analyzed from November 2025 to April 2026. Exposure Playing in at least 1 regular or postseason NFL game. Main Outcomes and Measures The main outcomes of this study were bias-adjusted prevalence of CTE neuropathology and all-cause dementia among the target population, both of which were measured in donors prior to this study. A cognitive symptom–related brain donation selection ratio (probability of donation given CTE divided by the probability of donation given no CTE) was estimated using Poisson regression and was applied to adjust donor-observed prevalence of CTE neuropathology at death and all-cause dementia during life. The prevalence estimates were adjusted for bias using the estimated selection ratio. Results The cohort consisted of 2362 deceased former NFL players (mean [SD] years played, 5.1 [3.9]; 971 [41.1%] aged ≥80 years at death), of whom 396 were brain donors and 1966 were nondonors. Of 387 donors, 362 (93.5%) had CTE. The median selection ratio was 4.97 (95% CI, 4.72-5.26). Bias-adjusted population prevalence of CTE at death was 74.5% (95% CI, 69.6%-78.3%), with a conservative lower-bound analysis estimating 63.7% (57.2%-68.9%). Bias-adjusted population prevalence of all-cause dementia history during life was 27.2% (95% CI, 22.6%-31.6%). Conclusions and Relevance The findings of this cross-sectional study suggest that selection bias materially inflates donor-based prevalence estimates but is unlikely to fully explain the high burden of CTE neuropathology among this population. Further research is required to understand the clinical impact of this disease.

item.title: Effectiveness of the mRNA-1345 Vaccine Against Respiratory Syncytial Virus in US Veterans

Lei Yan
Yuli Li

Robert Vergun
Vyshnika Sriskantharajah
Denise M. Hynes

item.description:
Authors: David P. Bui, Lei Yan, Yuli Li, Nallakkandi Rajeevan, Robert Vergun, Vyshnika Sriskantharajah, Denise M. Hynes, Kristin Berry, et al.
Journal: JAMA Network Open; Volume: 9; Issue: 10; Pages: e2640981
Abstract: Importance In clinical trials, the messenger RNA (mRNA)–1345 vaccine provided protection against respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) illness. Data on mRNA-1345 effectiveness in broader patient populations are needed. Objective To estimate the effectiveness of mRNA-1345 vaccination during a single respiratory illness season. Design, Setting, and Participants This cohort study used a target trial emulation framework to assess veterans 50 years and older receiving care in the Veterans Health Administration. Eligible vaccine recipients were matched with up to 4 unvaccinated individuals in 4 monthly, nested, sequential trials from October 1, 2025, to January 31, 2026. Outcomes were ascertained through May 31, 2026, or 24 weeks. Exposure A single dose of mRNA-1345 RSV vaccine vs no RSV vaccination. Main Outcomes and Measures The primary outcome was any positive RSV test result from day 14 after the matched index date. Secondary outcomes included RSV-associated emergency department (ED) or urgent care (UC) encounters and RSV-associated hospitalizations. Vaccine effectiveness was estimated as 100 × (1 – risk ratio). A sensitivity analysis comparing veterans who received same-day mRNA-1345 and influenza vaccination to influenza vaccination alone (active comparator arm) was performed to explore potential bias from differences in health care–seeking behavior and outcome ascertainment between comparator groups. Results A total of 74 926 vaccinated veterans were matched to 286 425 unique control individuals, weighted to represent 74 926 individuals, for a total of 149 852 study participants (median [IQR] age, 73.0 [63.3-78.6] years; 136 756 [91.3%] male). During a median (IQR) follow-up of 160 (130-168) days, estimated vaccine effectiveness was 60.3% (95% CI, 49.0%-70.4%) against any documented infection, 60.2% (95% CI, 47.2%-71.5%) against RSV-associated ED or UC encounters, and 81.8% (95% CI, 58.1%-99.9%) against RSV-associated hospitalizations. Estimated effectiveness against documented infections decreased with increasing age, from 82.9% (95% CI, 64.0%-96.7%) in the 50- to 59-year age group to 28.6% (95% CI, −12.0% to 60.4%) in the 80-year or older age group. With an active comparator arm, estimated effectiveness was 67.1% (95% CI, 48.9%-82.6%) against documented RSV infections, 69.5% (95% CI, 49.7%-85.4%) against RSV-associated ED and UC encounters, and 86.9% (95% CI, 56.5%-100.0%) against RSV-associated hospitalizations. Conclusions and Relevance In this cohort study using a target trial emulation of mRNA-1345 vaccine effectiveness during 24 weeks, vaccination was associated with protection against RSV illness and associated health care use in adults 50 years and older. Comparative effectiveness studies are needed to determine the relative benefits of available RSV vaccine products.

Authors: Casper Simonsen, Pieter de Heer, Simon Nørskov Thomsen, Rikke Krabek, Sarah Thorsen-Streit, Mark Preben Printz Lyngbæk, Anna Sundberg, Anne Sofie Knust Hjort, et al.
Journal: JAMA Network Open; Volume: 9; Issue: 10; Pages: e2640136
Abstract: Importance Physical deterioration and disease progression during neoadjuvant treatment can preclude tumor surgery in patients with gastroesophageal cancer. Whether preoperative exercise training can increase the probability of undergoing tumor surgery remains unknown. Objective To compare exercise training with usual care on the likelihood of not undergoing tumor surgery with curative intent after neoadjuvant treatment for gastroesophageal cancer. Design, Setting, and Participants PRESET-RCT was a single-blinded, parallel-group, 2-arm, superiority randomized clinical trial. Patients with gastroesophageal adenocarcinoma scheduled to undergo treatment with curative intent, including neoadjuvant treatment, and with no contraindication to exercise training were eligible. Participants were enrolled at University Hospital Copenhagen, Rigshospitalet, Copenhagen, Denmark, from August 16, 2018, to September 23, 2022, with final follow-up on October 22, 2024. Data analysis was performed from March 2023 to May 2025. Intervention The participants were randomized 1:1 to preoperative exercise training from diagnosis until tumor surgery or control. The intervention consisted of twice-weekly concurrent aerobic exercise and resistance training. Main Outcomes and Measures The primary outcome was not undergoing tumor surgery with curative intent. The secondary outcomes were treatment tolerance and overall survival. Results In total, 207 participants (73.7%) were randomized and 202 were included in the modified intention-to-treat analyses (mean [SD] age, 65.3 [8.5] years; 161 [78.9%] male; 170 [83.3%] with gastroesophageal junction cancer), with 101 randomized to each group. In the exercise group, 10 (9.9%) did not undergo tumor surgery with curative intent compared with 8 (7.9%) in the control group (odds ratio, 1.28; 95% CI, 0.48-3.38; P = .62). There were no between-group differences in permanent discontinuation of neoadjuvant treatment (odds ratio, 0.81; 95% CI, 0.38-1.72) or postoperative complications (odds ratio, 1.16; 95% CI, 0.61-2.20). The overall survival rates at 3 years for the exercise and control group were 51.0% and 65.0%, respectively (hazard ratio, 1.58; 95% CI, 1.02-2.45). Conclusion and Relevance In this randomized clinical trial, preoperative exercise training did not increase the likelihood of undergoing tumor surgery for patients with gastroesophageal cancer. The findings do not support the use of exercise training during neoadjuvant treatment to improve surgical outcomes, and further research is needed to determine its effects on long-term outcomes. item.description:
Authors: Sadaf Arefi Milani, Yong-Fang Kuo, Yong Shan, Eunice Park, Abisola Sotade, Huey-Ming Tzeng, Mukaila Raji
Journal: JAMA Network Open; Volume: 9; Issue: 10; Pages: e2640804
Abstract: Importance Medicare annual wellness visits (AWVs) may facilitate early diagnosis of Alzheimer disease and related dementias (ADRDs). However, it remains unclear whether AWVs lead to increased new prescriptions of dementia medications, including N -methyl- d -aspartate receptor antagonists (memantine) and acetylcholinesterase inhibitors (donepezil, rivastigmine, and galantamine). Objective To examine the association between incident AWVs and new dementia medication prescriptions. Design, Setting, and Participants This retrospective cohort study used 100% Medicare data for beneficiaries with ADRDs diagnosed from January 1 to December 31, 2018, who had continuous enrollment in Medicare Parts A, B, and D, from 3 years before to 1 year after the index date (January 1, 2018), excluding those enrolled in health maintenance organizations and with prior dementia medication prescriptions. Data analysis was performed from August 2025 to August 2026. Exposure Number of AWVs received in the 3 years before the index date (0, 1, 2, or ≥3). Main Outcomes and Measures Receipt of any dementia medication (yes or no). Results In this cohort of 799 268 Medicare beneficiaries with ADRDs (mean [SD] age, 82.3 [7.9] years; 64.5% female), 60.8% received no AWVs, 19.2% received 1 AWV, 12.9% received 2 AWVs, and 7.2% received 3 or more AWVs. New dementia medication prescriptions ranged from 9.8% to 14.1%, varying by number of AWVs received. After propensity score weighting, receipt of 1 AWV was associated with a 9.0% higher rate in dementia medication prescriptions (hazard ratio [HR], 1.09; 95% CI, 1.07-1.11), receipt of 2 AWVs was associated with a 12.0% higher rate (HR, 1.12; 95% CI, 1.10-1.14), and receipt of 3 or more AWVs was associated with a 16.0% higher rate (HR, 1.16; 95% CI, 1.13-1.19). An interaction between AWVs and prevalent cases of dementia was observed ( P for interaction = .009). For both incident and prevalent cases of dementia, a higher rate of dementia medications was associated with a higher number of AWVs, but those with incident dementia cases had larger increases. Conclusions and Relevance In this cohort study of Medicare beneficiaries with ADRD, an increasing number of AWVs received was associated with higher rates of new dementia medication prescriptions. These findings underscore the important role that AWVs may have in increasing the prescribing of medications that help manage symptoms of ADRD and suggest AWVs are essential to support quality dementia care (eg, symptom management) and advance care planning for future living arrangements.

item.title: Operational Challenges During Public Health Emergencies in Safety-Net Hospitals
item.dc:creator: Tara Kirk Sell
Vanessa Grégoire
Madisen S. Neufeld
Rachel R. Adler
Geoffrey Gosselin
Alysa Pomer
Biak L. Tial
Joel S. Weissman
item.description:
Authors: Tara Kirk Sell, Vanessa Grégoire, Madisen S. Neufeld, Rachel R. Adler, Geoffrey Gosselin, Alysa Pomer, Biak L. Tial, Joel S. Weissman, et al.
Journal: JAMA Network Open; Volume: 9; Issue: 10; Pages: e2640799
Abstract: Importance Safety-net hospitals (SNHs) serve as essential public health hubs, providing direct clinical care and critical social services to vulnerable populations, yet gaps persist in their ability to reliably deliver these essential services during disasters. Objective To identify common challenges faced by SNHs and actionable approaches described by participants to strengthen future emergency response capacity at these critical institutions. Design, Setting, and Participants For this qualitative study, from April through November 2025, key informant interviews were conducted with individuals across SNHs selected to represent a spectrum of SNH types. Thematic analysis of site-level case studies was used to identify cross-cutting and context-specific patterns across 5 domains: load balancing, staffing needs, supply chain, crisis standards of care (CSC), and health care coalitions (HCCs). Main Outcomes and Measures Stakeholder perspectives of pandemic preparedness, response, and recovery were evaluated to understand strategies to mitigate future health care disasters. Results Analysis of interviews with 69 individuals from 10 SNH sites identified systemic vulnerabilities across all 5 domains in SNHs. SNHs rarely succeeded in transferring critically ill patients without extensive staff time spent setting up the transfer. SNHs often experienced severe workforce disruptions from limited staff pools and nurse attrition, leaving them dependent on temporary staff at higher costs. Just-in-time personal protective equipment procurement and constricted manufacturing supply chains created supply crises. Few SNHs implemented full CSC, but many worked to find creative solutions to prevent more extensive changes in care standards. Opinions on written CSC were mixed, with some preferring structured frameworks and others preferring flexibility. Experiences with HCCs varied widely, with SNHs embedded in well-resourced HCCs reporting better coordination and support. Conclusions and Relevance In this qualitative study of SNH preparedness and response, findings indicated that SNHs faced challenges with load balancing, supply chain, staffing, CSC, and HCCs. To address such challenges in the future, SNHs, regional coalitions, and the federal government should implement sustainable changes that can be rapidly brought to bear in an emergency. Potential solutions may have outsized benefit for SNHs; however, such solutions must be designed to be accessible to SNHs and feasible in these settings.

Journal: JAMA Network Open; Volume: 9; Issue: 10; Pages: e2640893
Abstract: Importance Concerns about adolescent smartphone use and mental health have prompted many schools to implement mobile phone bans, but evidence of their effects remains mixed. Objective To examine whether schoolwide mobile phone bans were associated with changes in mental health and associated social and behavioral outcomes among adolescents in Iceland. Design, Setting, and Participants This repeated cross-sectional study used difference-in-differences analyses of data from 70 schools across 3 waves of the nationwide Youth in Iceland school survey. The surveys were administered to adolescents aged 13 to 15 years in February 2016, February 2018, and November 2023. Analyses were conducted from February 1, 2025, to January 30, 2026. Exposure Schoolwide mobile phone bans prohibiting student phone use during school hours. Between 2018 and 2023, 22 of 70 schools implemented a phone ban. Main Outcomes and Measures Primary outcomes were depressive symptoms, anxiety, hostility, and mental well-being. Secondary outcomes were perceived peer support, screen use (social media use, gaming alone, gaming with friends, and video watching), and bullying (in person and cyberbullying). Results Among 23 938 adolescent observations across the 3 study years, 11 964 (50.0%) were boys; the mean (SD) age was 13.98 (0.82) years. In the postpolicy period from 2018 to 2023, schoolwide mobile phone bans were not associated with meaningful changes in depressive symptoms (β, 0.65 [95% CI, 0.01-1.30]), anxiety (β, 0.21 [95% CI, −0.08 to 0.50]), hostility (β, 0.23 [95% CI, −0.12 to 0.59]), and mental well-being (β, −0.52 [95% CI, −1.08 to 0.03]). Results were similar in gender-stratified analyses and for the secondary outcomes. Sensitivity analyses examining timing of implementation and more stringent phone restriction criteria were consistent with the main findings. Conclusions and Relevance In this repeated cross-sectional study of adolescents in Iceland, schoolwide mobile phone bans were not associated with meaningful changes in adolescent mental health or related social and behavioral outcomes. These findings suggest that school phone bans implemented in isolation may be insufficient to improve adolescent mental health at the population level.

item.description:
Authors: Xin Hu, Changchuan Jiang, Xuesong Han, Lu Zhang, Piaopiao Li, Francisco J. Pasquel, Jane L. Meisel, Jacqueline B. Vo, et al.
Journal: JAMA Network Open; Volume: 9; Issue: 10; Pages: e2640781
Abstract: Importance Glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1 RAs) are increasingly used to treat type 2 diabetes, yet little is known about its utilization patterns in patients with cancer history, given limited oncology-specific guidance. Objective To evaluate trends and factors associated with GLP-1 RA use among Medicare beneficiaries with type 2 diabetes, comparing those with and without cancer history. Design, Setting, and Participants This retrospective cohort study used Surveillance, Epidemiology, and End Results–Medicare linked data to identify patients diagnosed with 7 common cancers in 2010 to 2021 and preexisting type 2 diabetes before cancer diagnosis. A noncancer cohort with type 2 diabetes was identified from a 5% random sample of Medicare beneficiaries and matched 1:1 to patients with cancer based on sociodemographic characteristics; controls were assigned a pseudo–index date corresponding to their matched patient’s cancer diagnosis date. Beneficiaries were followed up annually until death or December 31, 2022, for TM or December 31, 2021, for MA. Data were analyzed from December 2025 to July 2026. Exposures Diagnosis of 1 of 7 common cancers. Main Outcomes and Measures Any GLP-1 RA use. Proportions of beneficiaries with any GLP-1 RA use annually were stratified by traditional Medicare (TM) and Medicare Advantage (MA). Multivariable logistic regression examined (1) differences in GLP-1RA use between cancer and noncancer cohorts with and without adjusting for sociodemographic characteristics and comorbidities and diabetes-related complications; (2) cancer-specific factors associated with GLP-1RA use among the cancer cohort after 2018. Results A total of 373 278 Medicare beneficiaries (mean [SD] age, 76.1 [6.6] years; 188 746 [50.6%] female) with cancer and diabetes and 373 278 noncancer controls (153 358 unique beneficiaries) were included. GLP-1 RA use increased from 85 beneficiaries (0.5%) to 9083 beneficiaries (8.2%) and from 138 beneficiaries (0.9%) to 9300 beneficiaries (6.2%) in the cancer and noncancer cohorts, respectively, from 2010 to 2022 under TM; a similar increase was observed under MA. Despite higher unadjusted GLP-1 RA use among the cancer cohort than the noncancer cohort (probability difference, TM: 1.19 [95% CI, 0.94 to 1.44] percentage points [pp]; P &amp;lt; .001; MA: 0.45 [95% CI, 0.21 to 0.68] pp, P &amp;lt; .001), adjusted analysis showed no significant differences in GLP-1 RA use under TM (adjusted probability difference, 0.16 [95% CI, −0.10 to 0.41,] pp; P = .22) and lower use among cancer cohort under MA (−0.52 [95% CI, −0.76 to −0.28] pp; P &amp;lt; .001). Complications or comorbidities, including obesity (adjusted probability difference, TM: 3.35 [95% CI, 3.10 to 3.61] pp; P &amp;lt; .001; MA: 2.42 [95% CI, 2.19 to 2.64] pp; P &amp;lt; .001), dyslipidemia (adjusted probability difference, TM: 2.26 [95% CI, 2.03 to 2.50] pp; P &amp;lt; .001; MA: 1.80 [95% CI, 1.57 to 2.03] pp; P &amp;lt; .001), neuropathy (adjusted probability difference: TM: 3.91 [95% CI, 3.64 to 4.19] pp; P &amp;lt; .001; MA: 3.17 [95% CI, 2.94 to 3.41] pp; P &amp;lt; .001), retinopathy (adjusted probability difference, TM: 2.02 [95% CI, 1.78 to 2.27] pp; P &amp;lt; .001; MA: 1.84 [95% CI, 1.63 to 2.06] pp; P &amp;lt; .001), and chronic kidney disease (adjusted probability difference, TM: 2.01 [95% CI, 1.76 to 2.26] pp; P &amp;lt; .001; MA: 1.63 [95% CI, 1.40 to 1.85] pp; P &amp;lt; .001) were associated with greater likelihood of GLP-1RA use. Within the cancer cohort, breast (adjusted probability difference, TM: 1.05 [95% CI, 0.43 to 1.66] pp; P = .001; MA: 0.89 [95% CI, 0.37 to 1.41] pp; P = .001), gynecologic (adjusted probability difference, MA: 1.13 [95% CI, 0.45 to 1.81] pp; P = .001), and prostate (adjusted probability difference, TM: 1.30 [95% CI, 0.72 to 1.88] pp; P &amp;lt; .001; MA: 1.07 [95% CI, 0.56 to 1.58] pp; P &amp;lt; .001) cancers were associated with higher GLP-1 RA use than colorectal cancer, while pancreatic cancer was associated with lower GLP-1 RA use (adjusted probability difference, TM: −2.55 [95% CI, −3.17 to −1.93] pp; P &amp;lt; .001; MA: −1.64 [95% CI, −2.23 to −1.05] pp; P &amp;lt; .001). Conclusions and Relevance In this retrospective study of Medicare beneficiaries with type 2 diabetes, GLP-1 RA use increased substantially and primarily was associated with metabolic risk profile, with limited associations with cancer status. Variation across cancer types and stages suggests oncologic context may influence prescribing.

item.description:
Authors: Chengjie Xiong, Jingqin Luo, Ruijin Lu, Sarah Hartz, Walter Kukull, Suzanne E. Schindler, Joyce E. Balls-Berry, Jason Hassenstab, et al.
Journal: JAMA Network Open; Volume: 9; Issue: 10; Pages: e2640868
Abstract: Importance The underlying mechanisms for the paradox of higher prevalence of dementia but lower prevalence of amyloid positivity in self-identified Black US residents than White US residents remain unknown and are important for designing and analyzing prevention and treatment trials of Alzheimer disease. Objective To assess whether the age of mean amyloid onset (AMAO) explains the paradox of the reported racial differences in dementia and amyloid positivity. Design, Setting, and Participants This was a retrospective, multicenter, longitudinal cohort study with harmonized amyloid positron emission tomography (PET) and clinical data from self-identified Black and White individuals who were middle-aged or older across 5 academic institutes in the US conducting studies of memory and aging. The study was conducted from June 2020 to March 2026. Exposures Self-identified race, vascular comorbidities, sex, age, educational attainment, and apolipoprotein E ε4 carrier status. Main Outcomes and Measures Amyloid PET centiloid and cognition measured as a global cognitive composite constructed by averaging z scores across at least 6 cognitive tests in self-identified Black and White participants. Both cross-sectional and longitudinal analyses were conducted to compare racial groups in amyloid burden and cognition. Data were also analyzed using propensity score–matching of 2:1 (White:Black) by main covariates. Results Of 2653 participants (mean [SD] age, 69.0 [8.8] years; 1574 [59.3%] female), 406 (15.3%) were Black and 2247 (84.7%) were White. Black participants had a delayed AMAO compared with White participants in the unmatched (83.86 [95% CI, 76.55-91.35] years vs 71.38 [95% CI, 67.74-73.17] years; difference, 12.48 [95% CI, 5.03-22.28 years) and covariate-matched (85.17 [95% CI, 80.16-91.38] years vs 72.61 [95% CI, 70.79-74.55] years; difference, 12.57 [95% CI, 7.25-19.54] years) analyses. Although Black participants had a lower overall prevalence of amyloid positivity than White participants (24.1% vs 31.7%, P = .002), they had a higher prevalence of amyloid positivity than White participants in almost every interval of expected years to amyloid onset (EYAO, defined as participants’ simple chronological age minus the group-specific AMAO), hence Simpson’s paradox, (eg, −15 to −10 years for Black minus White prevalence in the unmatched cohort, 15.30 percentage points [95% Wilson CI, 0.06-0.26]). No significant racial differences were found in the longitudinal rate of amyloid accumulation after adjusting for the covariates either before the AMAO (eg, unmatched cohort Black minus White difference in slope per year, −0.28 [95% CI, −0.64 to 0.08]; P = .13) or after the AMAO (eg, unmatched cohort Black minus White difference in slope, −1.23 [95% CI, −3.05 to 0.60]; P = .17). Black participants had a higher prevalence of vascular comorbidities than White participants (56.9% vs 39.3%; P &amp;lt; .001), and Black but not White participants showed significant cognitive decline before the AMAO (Black minus White difference in slope per year, −0.016 (95% CI, −0.028 to −0.004)]; P = .009). Conclusions and Relevance This cohort study found that Black participants had delayed AMAO compared with White participants, partially explaining the paradox of the reported racial differences in prevalence of amyloid positivity and dementia. This finding suggests that EYAO may be an important confounder to analyze racial differences and may serve as a better (than age) inclusion or exclusion criterion to improve the representation of Black US residents in clinical trials of Alzheimer disease.

Abstract: Importance Evidence regarding the effectiveness of physical activity (PA) policies within preschool settings remains limited. Objective To evaluate the effectiveness of a cocreated preschool-level PA policy on children’s accelerometer-measured PA during preschool hours. Design, Setting, and Participants This single-blind, parallel-group, cluster randomized clinical trial was performed at public preschools in Stockholm, Sweden. Of 156 randomly sampled preschools invited, 124 were randomized. Children aged 3 to 5 years with parental consent were recruited from September 14 to December 11, 2020, baseline measurements from September 23, 2020, to January 22, 2021, and 6-month follow-up from March 8 to June 11, 2021. Statistical analyses were performed from March 6, 2023, to October 25, 2024. Intervention A cocreated preschool-level PA policy implemented for 6 months vs usual practice. Main Outcomes and Measures Prespecified primary outcomes were between-group differences in change in moderate to vigorous PA, total PA, and steps during preschool hours, measured using wearable accelerometers. Results Among 3751 children (mean [SD] age, 4.44 [0.86] years; 1934 male [51.6%]), 1960 attended intervention preschools and 1791 attended control preschools. All 124 preschools completed follow-up; data were available for 1530 children (78.1%) in intervention schools at baseline and 1435 (73.2%) at follow-up and 1430 children (79.8%) in control schools at baseline and 1356 (75.7%) at follow-up. Intention-to-treat analyses included 3417 children (1770 intervention and 1647 control). Moderate to vigorous PA increased from 27.4 to 33.0 minutes per day in the intervention group and from 27.6 to 33.0 minutes per day in the control group (difference in change, 0.3 [95% CI, −0.7 to 1.3] minutes per day; P = .57). Total PA increased from 177.7 to 185.3 minutes per day in the intervention group and from 176.5 to 184.5 minutes per day in the control group (difference, −0.3 [95% CI, −3.3 to 2.7] minutes per day; P = .84). Steps increased from 5415 to 5953 per day in the intervention and from 5549 to 6078 per day in the control groups (difference, 8 [95% CI, −118 to 133] steps per day; P = .90). No participants withdrew because of adverse events. Conclusions and Relevance In this cluster randomized clinical trial, a cocreated preschool PA policy did not increase children’s PA beyond usual practice after 6 months. These findings highlight the complexity of translating policy adoption into measurable behavioral change and of detecting such change in preschool settings. item.title: Prescribing SGLTis and GLP-1 RAs for Patients With Type 2 Diabetes, Guideline Updates, and Longitudinal Knowledge Assessment Scores

item.description:
Authors: Bradley M. Gray, Jonathan Vandergrift, Bruce E. Landon, Rozalina McCoy
Journal: JAMA Network Open; Volume: 9; Issue: 10; Pages: e2640858
Abstract: Importance Sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitors (SGLT2is) and glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1 RAs) reduce cardiovascular and kidney events in patients with type 2 diabetes (T2D) who have established atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease, heart failure, or chronic kidney disease, yet prescribing to these patients remains low. Objectives To describe temporal patterns in SGLT2i and GLP-1 RA prescribing before and after the 2019 American Diabetes Association (ADA) guideline update and to assess whether these patterns differed across physicians with subsequently measured different first-year American Board of Internal Medicine Longitudinal Knowledge Assessment (LKA) scores. Design, Setting, and Participants This serial cross-sectional study was conducted from October 2025 through January 2026, using 2017 to 2022 traditional Medicare claims. Endocrinologists first participating in the 2022 to 2023 LKA and the Medicare beneficiaries with T2D they treated were included. Exposure Time relative to the 2019 ADA guideline update. Main Outcomes and Measures The annual patient-year SGLT2i and GLP-1RA guideline-targeted and nontargeted patient fill rates were the main outcome. Linear physician, year, and target subgroup fixed-effects regression models were estimated, with patient demographic and health risk controls to evaluate within-physician associations between guideline-targeted vs nontargeted patient-year fill rates each year relative to 2018 (the year before the guideline update). The variation in these associations across first-year LKA score quartiles was also evaluated. Results A total of 1061 endocrinologists caring for 177 284 Medicare beneficiaries with T2D (mean [SD] age, 74.5 [6.1] years; mean [SD] 54.4% [49.8] female; mean [SD] 9.3% [29.1] Black, 6.6% [24.9] Hispanic, and 76.2% [42.6] White non-Hispanic) were included. Adjusted guideline-targeted SGLT2i and GLP-1 RA fill rates increased monotonically from 2018 to 2022 by 11.4 percentage points (pp) (95% CI, 10.5 to 12.3 pp; P &amp;lt; .001) and 2.4 (95% CI, 1.4 to 3.3 pp; P &amp;lt; .001) for SGLT2is and GLP-1 RAs targeted vs nontargeted subgroups, respectively. The associated SGLT2i increase was 3.9 pp (95% CI, 1.4 to 6.5 pp) larger for patients of endocrinologists with top vs bottom LKA quartile scores ( P = .003), but for GLP-1 RAs, this association was not statistically significant with wide confidence intervals. Conclusions and Relevance In this cross-sectional study, 2019 ADA guideline update timing was associated with substantially increased SGLT2i and moderately increased GLP-1 RA guideline-concordant prescribing among guideline-targeted, compared with nontargeted, patient subgroups by 2020. These increases in SGLT2i guideline congruent prescribing were associated with higher subsequently measured first-year LKA scores.

item.title: Food Insecurity Among Resident Physicians and Clinical Fellows at a Large Academic Medical Center
item.dc:creator: Erin Mahan
Atalay Demiray
Stephen J. Huot
June Criscione
Marietta Vazquez
item.description:
Authors: Erin Mahan, Atalay Demiray, Stephen J. Huot, June Criscione, Marietta Vazquez
Journal: JAMA Network Open; Volume: 9; Issue: 10; Pages: e2640774
Abstract: Importance Food insecurity is associated with adverse health and affects approximately 1 in 5 US medical students. A recent multi-institutional study found food insecurity in 14% of graduate medical education trainees using a 2-item screen; prevalence by the 10-item US Department of Agriculture Adult Food Security Survey Module remains poorly characterized. Objective To estimate reported food insecurity prevalence among resident physicians and clinical fellows and identify affected subgroups and barriers. Design, Setting, and Participants In this cross-sectional, anonymous electronic survey at the Yale New Haven Health System, all physicians in accredited postgraduate training were eligible (approximately 600). The survey was fielded August 7, 2023, to May 19, 2026, and responses arrived through November 2025 (121 of 165 [73%] in 2023). Exposures Year of training (including postgraduate year 1 [PGY-1] status) and self-reported barriers to obtaining food. Main Outcomes and Measures Food insecurity, a score of 3 or higher on the 10-item US Department of Agriculture module; prevalences and associations reported with 95% CIs. Results Of approximately 600 eligible trainees, 165 (28%) participated; 164 had complete food security data (53 PGY-1, 34 PGY-2, 23 PGY-3, 32 PGY-4, 22 other, including fellows). Overall, 50 of 164 respondents (30.5%; 95% CI, 24.0%-37.9%) met criteria for food insecurity. PGY-1 prevalence (24 of 53 [45.3%]) was approximately twice that of later years (26 of 111 [23.4%]; odds ratio [OR], 2.71; 95% CI, 1.35-5.43; P = .004). Lack of money was associated with food insecurity (45 of 60 [75.0%] vs 4 of 100 [4.0%]; OR, 72.00; 95% CI, 22.61-229.30; P &amp;lt; .001), whereas lack of time was not (OR, 1.24; 95% CI, 0.61-2.49; P = .55). PGY-1 trainees more often endorsed lack of money (27 of 52 [51.9%] vs 33 or 108 [30.6%]; OR, 2.45; 95% CI, 1.24-4.85; P = .009). Prevalence by specialty ranged from 5 of 26 (19.2%) to 5 of 10 (50.0%) ( P = .24). Conclusions and Relevance In this cross-sectional study of 164 resident physicians and clinical fellows, approximately one-third of respondents reported food insecurity, with the highest burden among PGY-1 trainees, whose recall window spanned the transition from medical school into residency, and an association with lack of money. Financial supports targeted to that transition warrant prospective evaluation.

item.title: Enteric Fever and Antimicrobial Resistance
item.dc:creator: Christan H. Stager
Layne Dorough
Molly Steele
Felicita Medalla
Jared L. Reynolds
Kristen Heitzinger
Hayat Caidi
Kaitlin A. Tagg
item.description:
Authors: Christan H. Stager, Layne Dorough, Molly Steele, Felicita Medalla, Jared L. Reynolds, Kristen Heitzinger, Hayat Caidi, Kaitlin A. Tagg, et al.
Journal: JAMA Network Open; Volume: 9; Issue: 10; Pages: e2640971
Abstract: Importance Increasing antibiotic resistance in enteric fever (typhoid or paratyphoid fever) is a global public health threat. Knowledge of current antimicrobial resistance patterns and identification of factors associated with acquiring resistant infections can help inform treatment and prevention decisions. Objective To estimate the prevalence of antimicrobial-resistant enteric fever in the US after the emergence of extensively drug-resistant Salmonella enterica Typhi in 2016 and describe characteristics of patients with resistant Salmonella Typhi or Paratyphi strains. Design, Setting, and Participants This cross-sectional, laboratory-based study included cases of culture-confirmed enteric fever diagnosed in the US. From January 2016 to December 2020, US health departments submitted epidemiologic data to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) through the National Typhoid and Paratyphoid Fever Surveillance (NTPFS) system, and public health laboratories submitted the corresponding Typhi or Paratyphi isolates to the CDC through the National Antimicrobial Resistance Monitoring System (NARMS). Initial data analysis was complete by March 31, 2023, and the antimicrobial resistance trends analysis was updated in August 2026. Exposures Patient variables collected by the NTPFS, including demographic characteristics, travel history, and typhoid vaccination status. Main Outcome and Measures Linked NTPFS-NARMS data from 2016 to 2020 were used to calculate the prevalence of antimicrobial resistance stratified by serotype and to conduct univariable logistic regression to estimate the associations of case characteristics and exposure variables with odds of infection with resistant strains. Results In this analysis, 2342 cases were included (1784 typhoid [76.2%], 426 paratyphoid A [18.2%], 114 paratyphoid B [4.9%], and 14 paratyphoid C [0.6%]; 4 isolates [0.2%] had unspecified paratyphoid serotypes). The median patient age was 25 years (IQR, 11-37 years), and patients were male in 1215 of 2325 cases (52.3%). Most patients reported traveling or residing internationally within 30 days of illness onset (1853 of 2217 [81.9%]). From 2016 to 2020, 1635 enteric fever isolates underwent susceptibility testing through NARMS; most Typhi (1061 of 1354 [78.4%]) and Paratyphi A (258 of 274 [94.2%]) isolates were not susceptible to ciprofloxacin. Among 1354 Typhi isolates, resistance exceeded 15% for ampicillin, for chloramphenicol, and for trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole and was 5.5% (74 isolates) for ceftriaxone; 1 Typhi isolate (0.1%) was resistant to azithromycin. Resistance to these agents was not observed among Paratyphi isolates. Conclusions and Relevance In this cross-sectional study, most typhoid and paratyphoid infections were not susceptible to ciprofloxacin, suggesting that ciprofloxacin should be avoided as empiric therapy for most travel-associated enteric fever cases. Cases of ceftriaxone-resistant typhoid fever were also observed. These findings suggest that treatment of enteric fever should be tailored to susceptibility test results.
